statement: In US adults prescribed opioid painkillers — veterans in Veterans Health Administration care in 2004–2009 (mostly men; 2,400 overdose deaths in a case-cohort of 422,786 people) and privately insured people aged 18–64 in 2001–2013 (315,428 people) — time with a filled benzodiazepine prescription, compared with time on opioid prescriptions alone, is associated with more overdoses. Among the veterans, overdose deaths (any drug, any intent) occurred at 316 per 100,000 person-years during benzodiazepine prescription against 71 with none (unadjusted); the adjusted hazard ratio was 3.86 (95% CI 3.49–4.26), and 2.33 (2.05–2.64) for periods after a benzodiazepine prescription had ended. During benzodiazepine prescription the adjusted hazard rose with the prescribed daily dose, to 3.06 (2.38–3.92) for the highest against the lowest of five dose groups. Among the insured adults, the adjusted yearly share with an emergency visit or hospital admission for opioid overdose was 2.42% with at least one day of overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions and 1.16% without (odds ratio 2.14, 2.05–2.24; 1.42 with occasional and 1.81 with long-term opioid prescriptions); that analysis did not adjust for opioid dose and counted only overdoses treated in hospital that people survived. Both studies measured pharmacy fills, not use; neither could see illicit drugs or medicines from other sources, or separate the medicine from the reasons it was prescribed (such as anxiety, depression or substance use), and the raised risk after prescriptions ended points to such differences or to continued use. Whether the combined risk exceeds what each drug carries alone was not tested, because everyone studied was receiving opioids; among the veterans the benzodiazepine association did not differ detectably by opioid dose (interaction P = 0.60). A third cohort, of North Carolina residents dispensed an opioid painkiller in 2010 (2,182,374 people, of whom 80.0% were also dispensed a benzodiazepine during the year), printed overdose death rates of 7.0 per 10,000 person-years with both medicines against 0.7 with opioid painkillers alone; it used no covariates, and its benzodiazepine rates do not fit its own counts, so it adds no estimate of size. Whether benzodiazepines cause the excess is not shown.
plain: Are opioids plus benzos (such as diazepam or alprazolam) more dangerous? In two large US studies of people prescribed opioid painkillers, people who also had a benzo prescription had more overdoses. Among US veterans, about 3 in 1,000 died of an overdose each year while a benzo was prescribed, against fewer than 1 in 1,000 without one, and the risk was higher with higher prescribed benzo doses. Among insured adults aged 18 to 64, about 2 in 100 a year with both prescriptions went to hospital with an opioid overdose, against about 1 in 100 with opioids alone. The studies counted prescriptions, not what people actually took, and could not see street drugs. People given benzos often had more anxiety, depression or substance use problems, and the risk was also higher after their benzo prescription had ended, so part of the link may come from these differences rather than the medicine itself.
population: US adults with filled opioid painkiller prescriptions: veterans in Veterans Health Administration care, financial years 2004–2009 (case-cohort of all 2,400 overdose deaths and a 420,386-person random subcohort; 93% men, editors' calculation; methadone maintenance, buprenorphine and palliative or hospice care excluded) and privately insured adults aged 18–64 continuously enrolled in 2001–2013 (315,428; MarketScan claims; cancer excluded); and, as a qualifier, North Carolina residents dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010 (2,182,374; state prescription-monitoring and death records)
exposure: A filled benzodiazepine prescription during opioid prescription: current receipt by days' supply (veterans) or at least one day of overlap between benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions in a calendar year (insured adults)
comparator: Time on opioid prescriptions without a benzodiazepine prescription: person-time never or not yet prescribed one (veterans); person-years without overlap (insured adults)
outcome: Death from overdose of any drug and any intent (National Death Index; veterans); emergency-room visit or hospital admission coded as opioid overdose in people who survived (insured adults)
magnitude: Veterans (Park et al., 2015): unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years, scaled to the source population: no benzodiazepine 71 (95% CI 66–76), former receipt 187 (170–205), current receipt 316 (298–334); editors' calculation: a difference of 245 per 100,000 person-years, about 3.2 against 0.7 deaths per 1,000 person-years. Adjusted hazard ratios against none: current 3.86 (3.49–4.26), former 2.33 (2.05–2.64). Within current receipt, by daily dose as prescribed (diazepam equivalents; study conditions), against >0–10 mg: >10–20 mg 1.69 (1.42–2.01), >20–30 mg 2.34 (1.91–2.86), >30–40 mg 2.65 (2.10–3.33), >40 mg 3.06 (2.38–3.92). Hazard ratios for the highest against the lowest opioid dose group were similar without (3.30), after (3.00) and during (3.92) benzodiazepine prescription; interaction P = 0.60. Privately insured adults (Sun et al., 2017): adjusted annual share with a hospital-treated opioid overdose 2.42% (2.32–2.51) with against 1.16% (1.13–1.18) without overlap, odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.45% against 1.02%, OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic (more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply a year) 5.36% against 3.13%, OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); in a broader sample enrolled for at least 2 years, adjusted relative risks 1.66 (1.64–1.69) and 1.61 (1.58–1.63). North Carolina (Dasgupta et al., 2016; a qualifier, not used for size): of 2,182,374 residents dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010, 80.0% (1,747,166) were also dispensed a benzodiazepine in the past year; overdose death rates were printed as 7.0 (95% CI 6.3–7.8) per 10,000 person-years with benzodiazepines and opioid analgesics together against 0.7 (0.6–0.9) with opioid analgesics only, with no covariates (deaths involving an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role, as judged by medical examiners). Editors' calculation: if 80% of the 2,181,847 person-years had been exposed to benzodiazepines, a rate of 7.0 per 10,000 person-years would mean over 1,200 deaths, against 478 among patients (629 in all), so the printed rates do not fit the counts.

evidence.extracted: Of 2,182,374 North Carolina residents dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010, 478 died of an overdose involving one (0.022%), within 629 such deaths in all; there were 2,181,847 person-years of opioid analgesic exposure. A benzodiazepine had been dispensed in the past year to 80.0% (1,747,166) of opioid analgesic recipients. Overdose death rates were about ten times higher with benzodiazepines and opioids concurrently (7.0 per 10,000 person-years, 95% CI 6.3, 7.8) than with opioid analgesics only (0.7, CI 0.6, 0.9); against patients on the same opioid dose, the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years in the lowest dose group and 45.8 in the highest. Editors' calculation: if 80% of the 2,181,847 person-years were exposed to benzodiazepines, 7.0 per 10,000 person-years would mean over 1,200 deaths, more than the 478 among patients or the 629 in all; the paper does not say how benzodiazepine exposure was timed in the rates, and no covariate is used.

evidence.extracted: Benzodiazepine exposure was set for each person as any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study. Incidence rates and rate ratios came from Poisson regression with person-days at risk as the offset and generalized estimating equations; no covariate was used. The authors name as the greatest limitation of the study that patients at higher doses are likely to have more serious illness, say no additional covariate information was available to adjust for the likelihood of treatment, and say data on other confounders were not controlled for.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies ROBINS-E high on their cards: confounding by indication is not controlled (in the veteran study the hazard ratio after benzodiazepine prescriptions ended, 2.33, shows it may be large); the insured-adult analysis omits opioid dose and does not order the overlap and the overdose in time; both use fills, not use.

inconsistency.note: Same direction in both; the different sizes (hazard ratio 3.86 for deaths, odds ratio 2.14 for hospital-treated events) match different outcomes and adjustment sets.

indirectness.note: None as worded: each population, exposure definition and outcome is stated separately.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the veterans' adjusted hazard ratio (3.86) exceeds 2, but the remaining confounding (severity of the indication, unmeasured drug use) runs away from the null, as the raised hazard after prescriptions ended indicates (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the veterans' adjusted gradient by prescribed benzodiazepine dose (1.69 to 3.06) is in the data, but in a between-person comparison higher prescribed doses plausibly track the same severity that confounds the main contrast, as the authors themselves say.

grade.reasoning: Two records-based cohorts in different US populations, read in full; observational, so they start low. Risk of bias −1 (both ROBINS-E high: uncontrolled confounding by indication, no opioid-dose adjustment in the insured-adult analysis, prescriptions as a proxy for use). Inconsistency 0, indirectness 0 as worded, imprecision 0; publication bias not assessable. Large effect and dose–response not applied (see the domain notes); a reading that credited the veterans' adjusted dose gradient would give low, and the strict reading gives very low. Relation: is associated with; the veteran study's authors themselves describe benzodiazepines as possibly a marker of risk, and causal wording would need designs that separate the medicine from the reasons it is prescribed. Status: replicated, by two independent teams in different populations with different outcomes (deaths; non-fatal hospital events). The claim does not say that the risks add or multiply: the veteran paper reads its interaction test as showing additivity, which misreads a Cox product term, and no study read compared benzodiazepines without opioids. A third cohort, of North Carolina residents (Dasgupta et al., 2016), was read in full: its benzodiazepine comparison is crude (no covariates; ROBINS-E very high) and its benzodiazepine rates cannot be reproduced from its own counts, so it points the same way but serves only as a qualifier and counts neither toward the rating nor toward the status. A UK study of people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment is the subject of a separate answer.

statement: In the United States, benzodiazepines were named on the death certificate in 21.0% of opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 8.7% in 1999 and after a peak of 26.2% in 2010; in 2015–2017 the share was 21.7% of 122,940 deaths: about one in three deaths involving prescription opioids (33.3%) or methadone (32.4%), about one in six involving heroin (15.9%) or synthetic opioids such as fentanyl (17.4%), and 26.9% of women's against 19.2% of men's deaths. Death certificates under-record drugs (12% of drug poisoning deaths in 2017 had no specific drug named) and testing varies between states and years, so these shares are probably too low. The national certificate series for 2004–2011, drawn from the same national death records, gives benzodiazepines in 18.4% of opioid painkiller overdose deaths in 2004 and 31% in 2011, and opioids in 69% and 75% of benzodiazepine overdose deaths, with about 25% of overdose certificates naming no drug (Jones and McAninch). In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners who weighed toxicology, records and the circumstances of each death judged a benzodiazepine to be involved in 61.4% (386) of 629 deaths involving an opioid painkiller (24.0% of these 629 people had not been dispensed an opioid painkiller in the previous year), against 26.2% on national certificates that year for all opioid overdose deaths, a different set of deaths (Dasgupta et al.). In the records of people who had opioid prescriptions, larger shares of deaths happened while a benzodiazepine was prescribed: 1,185 of 2,400 overdose deaths (49%) among US veterans on opioid painkillers in 2004–2009, and 971 of 1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths (77.3%) among Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients in 1997–2013, against 56.4% of matched living controls. These shares describe how often the drugs occur together in deaths; on their own they do not show how much benzodiazepines add to the risk of dying.
plain: How often are benzos involved in opioid overdose deaths? On US death certificates, benzos were listed in about 21 of every 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from about 9 in 100 in 1999. They were listed more often when the opioid was a prescription opioid or methadone (about 1 in 3 deaths) than with heroin or fentanyl (about 1 in 6), and more often in women's deaths than in men's. Death certificates miss some drugs, so the real numbers are probably higher. In studies of people with opioid prescriptions, half of the overdose deaths among US veterans, and three in four accidental opioid deaths in Ontario, Canada, happened while a benzo was also prescribed. In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners who looked at the test results and the circumstances judged that benzos were involved in about 6 in 10 of the deaths that involved an opioid painkiller. These numbers show how often the drugs appear together in deaths, not how much benzos add to the risk.
population: People who died of opioid overdose: all US death certificates 1999–2017 (399,230 deaths; 122,940 in 2015–2017); US veterans on opioid analgesics who died of drug overdose, 2004–2009 (2,400); Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients who died an accidental opioid-related death, 1997–2013 (1,256); US drug overdose deaths naming an opioid analgesic or a benzodiazepine, 2004–2011, on national certificates (Jones and McAninch); North Carolina residents who died of an overdose involving an opioid analgesic, 2010 (629 deaths; Dasgupta et al.)
exposure: Benzodiazepine named on the death certificate (ICD-10 T42.4), judged involved by medical examiners (North Carolina), or prescribed at the time of death (veterans: current prescription; Ontario: dispensed in the 120 days before death)
comparator: None for risk (shares among deaths); for context, matched living opioid recipients in Ontario
outcome: Share of opioid overdose deaths involving benzodiazepines, by year, opioid type and sex; share of benzodiazepine overdose deaths involving opioids (national certificates, 2004–2011)
magnitude: US death certificates (Tori et al., 2020): benzodiazepine co-involvement in all opioid overdose deaths 8.7% (1999), 26.2% (2010), 21.0% (2017); 2015–2017: 26,728 of 122,940 (21.7%), men 19.2%, women 26.9%; heroin 15.9% of 43,940, methadone 32.4% of 9,868, prescription opioids 33.3% of 41,709, synthetic opioids 17.4% of 57,459 (subtypes overlap); by state 5.4% to 45.5% (median 22.0%). Death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold from 1999 to 2017, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. Prescription records: US veterans on opioid analgesics, 1,185 of 2,400 overdose deaths (49%) during current benzodiazepine prescription (Park et al., 2015); Ontario, 971 of 1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths (77.3%) against 2,604 of 4,619 matched controls (56.4%) with a benzodiazepine dispensed in the prior 120 days (Gomes et al., 2017; descriptive, no adjusted estimate). National certificates 2004–2011 (Jones & McAninch, 2015): benzodiazepines named in 18.4% (2004) to 31% (2011) of opioid analgesic overdose deaths (p-trend < 0.0001), and opioids in 69% (2004) to 75% (2011) of benzodiazepine overdose deaths (p-trend = 0.0017); about 25% of overdose certificates name no drug. North Carolina 2010 (Dasgupta et al., 2016): a benzodiazepine judged involved by medical examiners in 386 of 629 overdose deaths involving an opioid analgesic (61.4%), of which 151 (24.0%) had no opioid analgesic dispensed in the previous 365 days; descriptive counts with no comparison group. Editors' calculation: 61.4% is 2.3 times the 26.2% named on national certificates for 2010 (a different set of deaths).

evidence.extracted: Deaths were counted only where an opioid analgesic was judged to have a primary or additive role, not where it was merely present; records were abstracted for decedents with toxicology results, 824 (92%) of the deaths identified. Editors' note: this is one state in one year, and the count says how often examiners judged a benzodiazepine involved, not how much it added to the risk of dying.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement could change the figures materially: certificate mentions depend on toxicology and reporting that vary by state and year (12–20% of drug poisoning deaths with no drug named), and prescription records do not show that the medicine was taken.

inconsistency.note: The figures differ (18% to 31% on certificates, depending on year and series; 61% judged by medical examiners in North Carolina; 49% and 77% with prescriptions) because they measure different things; all agree that benzodiazepines are common in opioid deaths.

indirectness.note: None as worded: each source's measure and population is stated.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it starts low and is never upgraded for size. Risk of bias −1 for measurement: death certificates under-record drugs and testing practices changed over the period, so the certificate shares are floors and their trend partly reflects reporting; the prescription-based shares come from two selected populations (VHA veterans; Ontario public-drug-plan recipients) and record dispensing, not use. statement: In the United States, alcohol was named on the death certificate in 14.7% of opioid overdose deaths in 2017 (12.4% in 1999; near 15% every year since 2008); in 2015–2017 the share was 15.0% of 122,940 deaths, 17.2% of men's and 10.5% of women's, similar in deaths involving heroin (16.5%), prescription opioids (14.2%) and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl (14.9%), lower with methadone (10.0%), and between 7.4% and 28.7% across states. Alcohol is under-recorded on death certificates, guidance on testing in opioid deaths does not address it, and reporting changed between states and years, so the true share may be higher and the trend is uncertain; in North Carolina in 2010, however, medical examiners judged ethanol involved in 12.2% (77) of 629 deaths involving an opioid painkiller (Dasgupta et al.), no higher than the certificate shares. Because the data contain nothing on how many people who use opioids also drink, they cannot show whether alcohol raises the risk of a fatal opioid overdose, or by how much; the correlation across states between binge drinking and the alcohol share of opioid deaths (r = 0.34) is an ecological association, not a finding about individuals. Two narrative reviews (Hickman et al., 2008; White & Irvine, 1999) set out the view that alcohol and opioids have additive or interactive effects on breathing, but describe no study in people that measured the combined effect. One cites post-mortem studies in which blood morphine was lower when blood alcohol was higher (60% lower above 100 mg/dl in two), says the effect at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated systematically, and lists other explanations for the same findings (lost tolerance, relapse, impaired judgement of tolerance, shared risk factors); the other cautions that post-mortem levels can vary with time after death and sampling site.
plain: How often is alcohol involved in opioid overdose deaths? On US death certificates, alcohol was listed in about 15 of every 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share that has changed little since 2008. It was listed in about 17 in 100 men's deaths and about 10 in 100 women's, and at similar rates whether the opioid was heroin, a prescription opioid or fentanyl. Alcohol is often left off death certificates, so the real share may be higher, although in one North Carolina study, where medical examiners judged each drug's part in the death, it was about 12 in 100 deaths involving an opioid painkiller. These numbers show how often alcohol appears in opioid deaths; because the study did not know how many people drink while using opioids, it cannot say how much alcohol adds to the risk of dying. Two reviews of the science say that alcohol and opioids both slow breathing and are expected to add up, but they describe no study in people that measured how much alcohol adds, and say the question is still open.
population: All US opioid overdose deaths certified in 1999–2017 (399,230; 122,940 in 2015–2017), CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death data
exposure: Alcohol named among the multiple causes of death on the certificate (ICD-10 T51.0 ethanol or T51.9 alcohol unspecified)
comparator: None: shares among deaths (state-level comparisons only)
outcome: Share of opioid overdose deaths with alcohol co-involvement, by year, opioid type, sex and state
magnitude: Alcohol co-involvement in all US opioid overdose deaths: 12.4% (1999), near 15% since 2008, 14.7% (2017). 2015–2017: 18,419 of 122,940 (15.0%); men 14,178 of 82,506 (17.2%), women 4,241 of 40,434 (10.5%); heroin 7,245 of 43,940 (16.5%), methadone 984 of 9,868 (10.0%), prescription opioids 5,936 of 41,709 (14.2%), synthetic opioids 8,584 of 57,459 (14.9%); by state 7.4% (Mississippi) to 28.7% (District of Columbia), median 13.3%. In 2017, alcohol-involved deaths numbered 0.7 per 100,000 persons with heroin, 1.3 with synthetic opioids, 0.7 with prescription opioids and 0.1 with methadone. Death rates for alcohol-involved opioid overdoses rose 5.5-fold from 1999 to 2017, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. Ecological correlation of state binge-drinking prevalence with the alcohol share, 2015–2017: r = 0.34 (P = .02). North Carolina 2010 (Dasgupta et al., 2016): ethanol judged involved by medical examiners in 77 of 629 overdose deaths involving an opioid analgesic (12.2%). Narrative reviews, second-hand figures with no sample sizes or years: alcohol detected in about 50% of heroin-related and about a third of methadone-related deaths; blood morphine 60% lower with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl than below it in two studies (United States, Australia) (Hickman et al., 2008).

evidence.extracted: Alcohol co-involvement in all US opioid overdose deaths rose from 12.4% in 1999 to 14.7% in 2017 and stayed near 15% from 2008; death rates for alcohol-involved opioid overdoses rose 5.5-fold from 1999 to 2017 (all opioid overdose deaths 5.0-fold). By subtype: heroin 10.3%–20.1% over the period and 15.5% in 2017 (0.7 deaths per 100,000); synthetic opioids 11.5% in 2013 to 14.9% in 2017 (1.3 per 100,000); prescription opioids 14.3%–15.4% in 2007–2017 (0.7 per 100,000 in 2017); methadone below 10% until 2017 (0.1 per 100,000).

evidence.extracted: Co-involvement is the mention of alcohol (T51.0 or T51.9) among the multiple causes on certificates of drug poisoning deaths with an opioid code. The authors state that alcohol is under-reported and often excluded from drug-related deaths, that the 2013 medical-examiner guidance does not address alcohol testing, that the 2006–2007 change in alcohol co-involvement may reflect 8 more states reporting and 481 extra alcohol-involved deaths reported by 8 others, that 12% of drug poisoning deaths in 2017 named no drug, that no individual-level data or blood levels were available, and that the counts are likely underestimated.

The authors state that the state-level correlations are not causal and may be prone to observational biases.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors report, from studies not read here, higher alcohol co-involvement with toxicology data: 22.3% of opioid deaths in Ontario, Canada (Gomes et al., 2017) and 18% alcohol-only co-intoxication in Massachusetts (Barocas et al., 2019); second-hand figures, cited only to show that certificate-based shares are lower.
evidence.quote: Alcohol remains an important and underrecognized cointoxicant in overdose deaths.

evidence.locator: Results > Overdose Deaths, 1st paragraph (p. 89)
evidence.extracted: In North Carolina in 2010, 629 deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role, as judged by medical examiners. Ethanol was involved in 12.2% (77) of them; heroin was present in 1.3% (8) and cocaine in 8.4% (53). Editors' note: one state in one year, among deaths involving an opioid painkiller and judged by medical examiners, so this is not a like-for-like test of whether certificates under-record alcohol.

evidence.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph (p. 1060); 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 1061)
evidence.extracted: A For Debate paper that presents no new data. From studies it cites without sample sizes or years: alcohol is the most commonly detected substance in heroin-related deaths (about 50%) and is detected in approximately a third of methadone-related deaths; several studies of heroin deaths report an inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem, with blood morphine 60% lower where blood alcohol was above 100 mg/dl than below it (United States and Australia). The authors give as the prevailing interpretation additive or interactive effects on breathing, and list other routes to the same findings: alcohol may impair judgement of tolerance, alcohol use is linked with heroin relapse, people reducing heroin may drink more so that falling tolerance could be the underlying problem, and polydrug use may mark people at risk for other reasons. They say the effect of alcohol with heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated systematically and that a pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic interaction remains unproven. Editors' note: the post-mortem limit that White and Irvine state is not mentioned in this paper.

evidence.locator: Factors determining susceptibility to opioid overdose > Metabolic factors, paragraph beginning 'It is also important to recognize' (p. 965); Opioid-drug interactions > Sedatives, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 968-969)
evidence.extracted: A narrative review. It says there is considerable evidence that many overdoses are due to the combined effects of opioids with other drugs, chiefly alcohol and benzodiazepines, but cites no source in that sentence and describes no study of alcohol with an opioid in people. It reasons from receptor pharmacology: alcohol and benzodiazepines are relatively weak breathing depressants on their own; alcohol acts at the GABA-A receptor complex, at a site other than the benzodiazepine site, and blocks NMDA receptors, effects that the review says should be at least additive with those of mu-receptor opioids. It advises that post-mortem drug measurements be treated with caution because levels vary with time after death, tissue sampled and body site, and post-mortem metabolism is possible.

risk_of_bias.note: Under-recording of alcohol on death certificates, no alcohol testing guidance, and reporting that changed by state and year could change both the level and the trend materially (JBI moderate on the study card).

inconsistency.note: One main data source; toxicology-based figures cited by the authors are higher (22.3% in Ontario, 18% in Massachusetts), but a North Carolina count of medical examiners' judgments (12.2%) is not, so under-recording is likely but not shown.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim describes certificate mentions in the United States and states what they do not show.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3) from one national death-certificate series; it starts low and is never upgraded. Risk of bias −1 for measurement (alcohol is under-recorded and testing and reporting changed over time and between states), so the shares are floors and the flat trend may partly reflect reporting. Inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision 0. Certainty very low for the exact share; the order of magnitude (about one in seven certified opioid deaths) is the study's finding. Status: single study; the North Carolina count covers deaths that are also in the national records, and the two narrative reviews are second-hand, so none is counted as a replication. The claim states plainly that these data say nothing about how much alcohol raises the risk of dying: that needs individual-level studies with a denominator, none of which has been read; the two narrative reviews were read and describe none.

verification.flag_note: No study read estimates the risk that alcohol adds to opioid overdose. Hickman et al. 2008 (Addiction, 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2008.02134.x) and White & Irvine 1999 (Addiction, 10.1046/j.1360-0443.1999.9479612.x), items 19 and 20 of the DOI list, are narrative reviews of that question, now read in full by AI reader 57: they give reasoning from receptor pharmacology and post-mortem patterns, and no measured risk (anchors ai-located: a second reader is needed; their study cards, and the Dasgupta et al. 2016 card whose North Carolina count is added, are staged in data/study-cards/_incoming/interactions/ and must be merged first); Gomes et al. 2017 on alcohol in Ontario opioid deaths (Drug Alcohol Depend, 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2017.07.008) gives toxicology-based figures.

statement: In adults in Ontario, Canada, who were dispensed opioid painkillers through the public drug plan (non-cancer pain; mostly under 65 and on low incomes; 1997–2013), a gabapentin prescription in the previous 120 days was associated with higher odds of accidental opioid-related death confirmed by the coroner: gabapentin had been dispensed to 12.3% of 1,256 people who died and 6.8% of 4,619 matched controls (adjusted odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.18–1.88, adjusted for opioid dose, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, alcohol use disorder and other factors). By prescribed daily gabapentin dose the adjusted odds ratios were 1.32 (0.89–1.97) for low, 1.56 (1.06–2.28) for moderate and 1.58 (1.09–2.27) for high doses, with widely overlapping intervals, so a dose–response relation is not shown; anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), used as a comparison expected to carry no added risk, gave 1.14 (0.98–1.32). In people receiving methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK general practice (1998–2014), a gabapentin or pregabalin prescription was not clearly associated with drug-poisoning death (hazard ratio 1.54, 0.60–3.98; 5 deaths) but was associated with deaths from other causes (1.83, 1.28–2.62), which suggests that the people prescribed these medicines differed in health from others. A research letter from the same Ontario team and data source (1997–2016) found a similar association for pregabalin: it had been dispensed in the previous 120 days to 4.9% of 1,417 people who died of an opioid-related cause and 3.0% of 5,097 matched controls (adjusted odds ratio 1.68, 1.19–2.36, adjusted for gabapentin, antidepressants, benzodiazepines and other sedating medicines, opioid dose and other factors); by prescribed daily dose the adjusted odds ratio was 1.52 (1.04–2.22) for low or moderate doses and 2.51 (1.24–5.06) for high doses, with overlapping intervals and no test of a trend, and the comparison with anti-inflammatory painkillers again gave 1.04 (0.90–1.19). The letter runs to three pages and has no limitations section, and its years overlap those of the gabapentin study, so the two Ontario analyses are not independent. The studies used dispensing records and did not know why gabapentin or pregabalin was prescribed or whether illicit drugs were used. Because everyone studied was taking opioids, neither Ontario analysis tests whether the combined risk exceeds what each medicine carries alone, and whether either medicine causes the excess deaths is not shown.
plain: Are gabapentin and pregabalin with opioids more dangerous? In one study in Ontario, Canada, of people getting opioid painkillers through the public drug plan, 12 in 100 people who died of an accidental opioid overdose had recently been given gabapentin, against about 7 in 100 similar people who did not die. After taking opioid dose and other medicines into account, the odds of an opioid death were about 1.5 times higher with gabapentin. Higher gabapentin doses were not clearly riskier than lower ones. A UK study of people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment found too few poisoning deaths to say, and people given gabapentin-type medicines there died more often of other causes, a sign that they were in poorer health. The studies did not know why these medicines were prescribed or whether people used street drugs. The same Ontario team found a similar link for pregabalin in a short report: about 5 in 100 people who died had recently been given it, against about 3 in 100 similar people who did not die, and the odds of an opioid death were about 1.7 times higher. It used the same kind of records and may include some of the same people.
population: Ontario public-drug-plan recipients of opioid analgesics for non-cancer pain, 1997–2013 (1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths and 4,619 matched living controls; 94% under 65; 42–44% in the lowest income fifth), and, for pregabalin, Ontario public-drug-plan recipients of opioids aged 15–105, 1997–2016 (1,417 opioid-related deaths and 5,097 matched living controls; 43% in the lowest income fifth); and, as a qualifier, 12,118 people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK primary care, 1998–2014
exposure: Gabapentin (2017 study) or pregabalin (2018 letter) dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (Ontario); a gabapentinoid (gabapentin or pregabalin) prescription during or up to 12 months after opioid agonist treatment (UK)
comparator: Opioid recipients without recent gabapentin or pregabalin (Ontario, matched controls); periods without a gabapentinoid prescription (UK)
outcome: Accidental opioid-related death confirmed by the coroner (Ontario, 2017 study); opioid-related death excluding suicide and homicide, with ascertainment not stated (Ontario, 2018 letter); drug-poisoning and other deaths from death registrations (UK)
magnitude: Ontario (Gomes et al., 2017): recent gabapentin in 155 of 1,256 cases (12.3%) and 313 of 4,619 controls (6.8%); unadjusted OR 1.99 (95% CI 1.61–2.47), adjusted OR 1.49 (1.18–1.88); supply overlapping the date of death, adjusted OR 1.46 (1.12–1.89). By prescribed daily dose (study conditions): low (<900 mg) 41 against 101 exposed, adjusted OR 1.32 (0.89–1.97); moderate (900–1,799 mg) 57 against 111, 1.56 (1.06–2.28); high (≥1,800 mg) 57 against 101, 1.58 (1.09–2.27); post hoc ≥2,500 mg 1.83 (1.04–3.22). Negative-control exposure, NSAIDs: adjusted OR 1.14 (0.98–1.32). Pregabalin, Ontario (Gomes et al., 2018): recent pregabalin in 69 of 1,417 cases (4.9%) and 153 of 5,097 controls (3.0%); unadjusted OR 1.85 (1.36–2.53), adjusted OR 1.68 (1.19–2.36); supply overlapping the index date 60 (4.2%) against 121 (2.4%), adjusted OR 1.81 (1.26–2.60); with controls also matched on recent use of other sedating medicines (1,199 cases, 3,935 controls) 59 (4.9%) against 116 (3.0%), adjusted OR 2.00 (1.39–2.88). By prescribed daily dose (study conditions): up to 300 mg 52 (3.7%) against 128 (2.5%), adjusted OR 1.52 (1.04–2.22); above 300 mg 17 (1.2%) against 25 (0.5%), 2.51 (1.24–5.06); no trend test. Negative-control exposure, NSAIDs: 531 cases against 1,830 controls, adjusted OR 1.04 (0.90–1.19). All models adjusted for gabapentin. No absolute risks (case–control design). UK OAT (Macleod et al., 2019): gabapentinoid co-prescription, drug-poisoning deaths 5 in 538 person-years (0.93 per 100) against 108 in 19,410 (0.56), adjusted HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98); other deaths 46 in 571 (8.06 per 100) against 239 in 19,815 (1.21), adjusted HR 1.83 (1.28–2.62); all causes adjusted HR 1.71 (1.33–2.20).

evidence.extracted: A population-based nested case–control study of Ontario residents eligible for public drug coverage who received prescription opioids between 1 August 1997 and 31 December 2016; the methods, data sources and analyses follow the authors' earlier gabapentin study, with differences described. Cases died of an opioid-related cause, excluding suicide and homicide; each was matched to up to 4 controls on age (within 3 years), sex, index year, history of chronic kidney disease and Charlson score, and conditional logistic regression was adjusted for characteristics still imbalanced after matching. After matching, cases were more likely than controls to have recent benzodiazepines (1,073, 75.7% against 2,735, 53.7%; standardized difference 0.45 against weighted controls), other CNS depressants (35.4% against 23.8%), long-acting opioids (51.4% against 36.3%) and opioid doses of 200 or more morphine milligram equivalents a day (27.0% against 16.2%); 43.0% of cases and 43.1% of controls were in the lowest income fifth. Editors' note: the letter does not say how opioid-related deaths were identified, and it has no limitations section.

evidence.locator: Discussion, single paragraph (p. 1); Grant Support (p. 2)
evidence.extracted: The authors read the result as compelling evidence for a potentially life-threatening drug-drug interaction between pregabalin and opioids, similar to that seen with gabapentin, note that more than half of Ontario residents starting pregabalin are also prescribed an opioid, and call for a revision of the pregabalin product monographs. The work was funded by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care. Editors' note: this reading is causal and goes beyond an adjusted odds ratio of 1.68 from dispensing records; the letter gives no reason for pregabalin prescribing.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded, a borderline judgment: the Ontario study is ROBINS-E some concerns (coroner-confirmed outcome, matching on a disease risk index, adjustment for opioid dose and other sedating medicines, a near-null negative control), with remaining concerns about the indication for gabapentin, gabapentin misuse and unmeasured drug use, which could make the true association smaller. The pregabalin letter (Gomes et al., 2018) is also ROBINS-E some concerns, with the same design, data and adjustment but no limitations section and an abbreviated description of methods. The UK qualifier is ROBINS-E high but carries no weight in the rating.

inconsistency.note: The UK estimate for drug-poisoning death points the same way but is too imprecise to test consistency, and comes from a different population; the pregabalin letter points the same way, from the same team and data source.

indirectness.note: None as worded: each finding is stated for its own medicine (gabapentin; pregabalin) with opioid painkillers in a public-plan population.

imprecision.note: The main interval (1.18–1.88) excludes no association; the pregabalin interval (1.19–2.36) is wider; the dose-specific and UK estimates are imprecise and the claim says so.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with two analyses from one team.

dose_response.note: Not applied: low, moderate and high doses gave 1.32, 1.56 and 1.58 with overlapping intervals and no trend test; the very-high-dose estimate is post hoc. For pregabalin, low or moderate prescribed doses gave 1.52 and high doses 2.51 (1.24–5.06) from 17 exposed cases, also with no trend test.

grade.reasoning: Two nested case–control analyses read in full (Ontario: a full paper on gabapentin and a three-page letter on pregabalin), observational, so they start low; not downgraded for risk of bias (ROBINS-E some concerns on the study card; borderline, see the domain note), inconsistency, indirectness or imprecision; not upgraded. Certainty low. A strict reader who judged unmeasured gabapentin misuse and drug use an important uncontrolled confounder would downgrade once to very low; the Ontario design is nonetheless the strongest among the prescription studies read in this batch, which is why this answer is rated higher than the one on benzodiazepines, whose studies are at high risk of bias. Relation: is associated with; the authors' reading of a life-threatening drug–drug interaction is causal and goes beyond adjusted odds ratios of 1.49 (gabapentin) and 1.68 (pregabalin) with an unclear dose pattern. Status: replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.4): the pregabalin letter repeats the gabapentin design in the same data source, with overlapping years and a different case definition and matching, so it is not independent. A strict reading would call the answer a single study and would rate the pregabalin part, a three-page letter whose methods refer back to the gabapentin paper, one level lower. The UK treatment cohort (gabapentin and pregabalin together) is a different population, has only 5 exposed drug-poisoning deaths and shows an excess in other deaths, so it neither replicates nor contradicts the finding.

statement: In 12,118 people aged 15–64 receiving methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK general practice (1998–2014; cause of death known for about 7,100 in England), periods with a prescribed benzodiazepine, during treatment or up to a year after it, compared with periods without, were associated with more deaths from drug poisoning: 1.06 against 0.45 deaths per 100 person-years (39 and 74 deaths); adjusted hazard ratio 2.96 (95% CI 1.97–4.43); 2.51 (1.57–4.01) at doses within and 4.57 (2.46–8.47) above the national formulary's recommended maximum; and similar during treatment (2.92) and in the year after it (2.92). In the same analysis, benzodiazepine prescriptions were not clearly associated with deaths from all causes (1.17, 0.97–1.42). Z-drug sleeping tablets (zopiclone, zolpidem, zaleplon) were also associated with drug-poisoning death (2.75, 1.57–4.83; 15 deaths), without a dose gradient. Treatment episodes with a benzodiazepine prescription lasted longer (adjusted mean 416 against 244 days), and benzodiazepine prescription during treatment was still associated with more drug-poisoning deaths when this was taken into account (3.34, 2.14–5.20). The analyses adjusted for age, sex, year, region, an index of 17 chronic illnesses and treatment type, but no mental-health, alcohol or illicit-drug measures are among the covariates, and such differences may explain part of the association; in the second analysis benzodiazepine prescription during treatment was also associated with deaths from other causes (1.73, 1.28–2.33), which weakens the authors' argument that the excess is specific to poisoning. Prescriptions from specialist services and non-prescribed sedatives were not recorded. Gabapentin and pregabalin are covered in the answer on gabapentinoids. Whether the prescriptions cause the excess deaths is not shown.
plain: Are benzos riskier for people on methadone or buprenorphine? In a large UK study of people getting methadone or buprenorphine from their family doctor, deaths from drug poisoning were about 1 in 100 people a year during times when a benzo was also prescribed, against about 1 in 200 at other times. The link was stronger when the prescribed benzo dose was above the recommended maximum, and it was similar during treatment and in the year after leaving it. Sleeping tablets called z-drugs (such as zopiclone) showed a similar link, but there were few deaths. People prescribed benzos stayed in treatment longer, and the link with poisoning deaths remained after taking this into account. The study did not take into account mental health, alcohol or street drug use, which may explain part of the link.
population: People aged 15–64 prescribed methadone or buprenorphine as opioid agonist treatment in UK general practice (CPRD), 1998–2014: 12,118 people, 36,126 person-years, 657 deaths; cause of death from ONS for 7,106 in England (113 drug-poisoning deaths)

outcome: Death from drug-related poisoning (ONS death registrations); deaths from all causes and from other causes; treatment episode duration

evidence.extracted: The authors describe a threefold increase in drug-related poisoning mortality with benzodiazepines, during and after treatment, and higher at doses above the formulary maximum; they acknowledge confounding by indication, that propensity scores added little in their earlier work, that no instrument was available and that non-prescribed sedatives could not be measured, and still call their result the strongest evidence that benzodiazepine co-prescription is itself a cause of drug-poisoning death.
evidence.quote: is of itself a cause of increased risk of death from DRP

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high on the study card: mental-health diagnoses, alcohol and illicit drug use (including non-prescribed benzodiazepines) were not measured, and adjustment for the measured factors moved the estimates away from the null; specificity to poisoning deaths differs between the paper's own analyses (other deaths 0.91 in Table 4, 1.73 in Table 6).

inconsistency.note: One study; the earlier Scottish study the authors describe points the same way but has not been read.

indirectness.note: None as worded: people in primary-care opioid agonist treatment in the UK.

imprecision.note: The benzodiazepine estimates rest on 39 exposed drug-poisoning deaths with intervals clear of no association; the z-drug estimate rests on 15 deaths and is stated with its count.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the adjusted hazard ratio (2.96) exceeds 2, but the unmeasured confounders (heavier illicit benzodiazepine and alcohol use, mental illness) would bias away from the null (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: hazard ratios of 2.51 within and 4.57 above the formulary maximum form a gradient, but prescribing above the maximum plausibly marks heavier benzodiazepine dependence, the same confounding as the main contrast.

grade.reasoning: One records-based cohort read in full; observational, so it starts low. Risk of bias −1 (ROBINS-E high: the confounders most likely to explain the association were not measured, and the paper's own tables disagree on whether the excess is specific to poisoning deaths). Inconsistency not assessable, indirectness 0 as worded, imprecision 0. Large effect and dose–response not applied (domain notes); a reading that credited the prescribed-dose gradient would give low, and the strict reading gives very low. Certainty very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors' description of benzodiazepines as of itself a cause goes beyond what the design shows. Status: single study for people in opioid agonist treatment; the US studies of people prescribed opioid painkillers (the answer on benzodiazepines with opioids) agree in direction but concern a different population.

statement: In the statistical models of the two studies read that measured both agents (a driving simulator, and records of drivers in fatal crashes), lane weave or the odds of a recorded unsafe driver action were higher with cannabis and alcohol together than with either alone, by about the sum of the two separate effects and not clearly more than the sum. In the simulator (18 healthy adults who smoke cannabis occasionally, driving after every condition in random order), lane weave rose with blood THC by 0.26 cm per µg/L (standard error 0.07) and with breath alcohol by 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (0.15), both modelled for the time of the drive, and no interaction term was selected; from a drug-free median of 31.4 cm, the model gives +1.3 cm for THC 5 µg/L, +2.1 cm for breath alcohol 0.05 g/210 L and +3.4 cm for both, while lane departures and lateral acceleration rose with alcohol but not with THC. Among 150,010 drivers of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks in fatal US crashes (1991–2008) with blood tests for alcohol and drugs, a police-recorded unsafe driver action was linked to both: for a 45-year-old man with no other drugs or driving record, about 64 in 100 had one at a blood alcohol of 0.05 g/100 mL without THC and 66 in 100 with it, and 70 and 71 in 100 at 0.08 (editors' calculation); the odds ratio for THC fell as alcohol rose, from 1.165 (95% CI 1.082–1.255) at 0.00 to about 1.09 at 0.05 and 1.05 at 0.08 (editors' calculation). Both studies differ from driving on a road. The simulator measured lane weave in healthy volunteers, its combined values are sums by construction, 18 people were analysed, and achieved THC overlapped between its two cannabis doses. The crash analysis compares drivers who were already in fatal crashes, with and without a recorded unsafe action, so it measures neither crash risk nor impairment; it rests on a yes/no blood result for THC in about one in five eligible drivers, and prints no test of what THC adds to alcohol at 0.05 or 0.08. A meta-analysis reports a higher odds ratio for the combination than for cannabis alone in every study that assessed it, without numbers, which does not separate additive from more-than-additive effects. Both papers describe other simulator and on-road studies as disagreeing on whether the combination exceeds the sum; these were not read. Neither paper reports how impaired the drivers felt, neither gives the risk to one driver, and cause is not shown.
plain: Does cannabis with alcohol make driving worse than either alone? In a driving simulator, 18 healthy adults weaved a little more in their lane with cannabis and a little more with alcohol. With both, the extra weave was about the two added together: 3.4 cm more with both (THC 5 µg/L in blood, breath alcohol 0.05), against 2.1 cm more with alcohol alone, on a usual weave of about 31 cm. In US records of drivers in fatal crashes who had a blood test, about 64 in 100 at a blood alcohol of 0.05 had a recorded unsafe driving action, and about 66 in 100 if cannabis was also found. At 0.08 it was about 70 and 71 in 100, so cannabis added less as alcohol rose. Neither study measured crash risk on real roads, and a positive cannabis test shows it was in the blood, not that a driver was impaired. Other studies disagree on whether the two together do more than the sum of each.
population: Adults who drive: 18 healthy adults aged 21–37 who smoke cannabis occasionally (driving-simulator study; 19 drove, one excluded after the fact), and 150,010 drivers aged 20 or older of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks in fatal US crashes, 1991–2008, who had blood tests for alcohol and drugs (149,006 in the main analysis)
exposure: Cannabis together with alcohol: vaporized cannabis with blood THC modelled for the time of the drive, and alcohol drunk before it (study conditions, simulator); a THC-positive blood test with blood alcohol 0.00–0.08 g/100 mL (crash records)
comparator: Alcohol alone, cannabis alone, or neither (placebo drive in the simulator; blood alcohol 0.00 with no THC detected in the crash records)
outcome: Lane weave in a driving simulator (standard deviation of lateral position, cm); a police-recorded potentially unsafe driver action among drivers in fatal crashes
magnitude: Driving simulator (Hartman et al., 2015; 18 healthy adults analysed of 19 who drove; lane weave as standard deviation of lateral position, SDLP; model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road; drug-free median 31.4 cm, between-person range 24.7–44.8): blood THC 5 µg/L +1.3 cm (4.1%); breath alcohol 0.05 g/210 L +2.1 cm (6.7%); both +3.4 cm (11%), the same as breath alcohol 0.08 alone (+3.4 cm); combined values are sums because the selected model has no interaction term. Alcohol, not THC, raised lane departures per minute (+35% at 0.05 g/210 L, +55% at 0.08) and maximum lateral acceleration in events without sharp turns (+9.5% and +15%); neither drug changed steering-angle variability. By administered condition (18 drivers each; study conditions; no tests or intervals given), mean SDLP was placebo 28.8 cm, alcohol alone 32.3 (+12%), low THC alone 31.3, high THC alone 31.2, low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%) and high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%); in a mixed model by achieved THC group the THC-by-alcohol term had P = 0.24 (low power, the authors say). Fatal-crash drivers (Dubois et al., 2015; 150,010 drivers with blood tests for alcohol and drugs, 149,006 in the main analysis; a recorded unsafe driver action as a proxy for responsibility; model for a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or driving record; share with an unsafe action calculated by the editors from the printed predicted odds): 52 in 100 at blood alcohol 0.00 without THC and 56 in 100 with THC; 64 and 66 in 100 at 0.05; 70 and 71 in 100 at 0.08. Odds ratios against no alcohol and no THC: THC alone 1.16 (1.08–1.26); alcohol 0.05 alone 1.66 (1.63–1.69) and with THC 1.81 (1.70–1.93); alcohol 0.08 alone 2.17 (2.11–2.23) and with THC 2.28 (2.13–2.44). The THC-by-blood-alcohol term was 0.987 (0.981–0.994) per 0.01, so the odds ratio for THC falls as alcohol rises: about 1.17 at 0.00, 1.09 at 0.05 and 1.05 at 0.08 (editors' calculation, no interval). The combined odds ratio is close to the sum of the two separate excesses (about 1.83 at 0.05 and 2.34 at 0.08, editors' calculation) and below their product (1.93 and 2.53). Asbridge et al. (2012): in every study that assessed cannabis with alcohol, the odds ratio for the combination was higher than for cannabis alone; no numbers are given.

grade.reasoning: Two sources of different kinds, both read in full. The real-world half rests on a records-based case-control analysis (starts low); the other on a within-person simulator study with randomized condition order, which would start high. The claim is rated from the weaker link, so it starts low. Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 (see the domain notes); inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0; large effect, dose-response and plausible confounding not applied. statement: In drivers, a positive test for recent cannabis, compared with a negative test, is associated with higher odds of being in a crash or of being judged responsible for one. Across 28 estimates from 21 case-control and culpability studies in 13 countries (1982–2015), the pooled odds ratio was 1.36 (95% CI 1.15–1.61) by random effects and 1.22 (1.10–1.36) by a regression that corrects for small-study effects (PEESE). A 2012 meta-analysis of nine studies reported 1.92 (1.35–2.73) from crude counts; for those nine studies the re-analysis found a lower value, which its authors say lies between the two pooled figures, after re-extracting counts, using adjusted estimates and correcting for the culpability design. The size depends on how alcohol was handled: 1.11 (1.04–1.18) and 1.18 (1.07–1.30) in the 14 estimates that controlled for alcohol, against 1.79 (1.28–2.51) and 1.69 (1.25–2.28) in the 14 that did not. Individual estimates range from 0.22 to 13.40, with 17 above 1 and 9 below (editors' count), and no heterogeneity statistic is printed. The heaviest single weight (10.68%) is a US analysis of 150,010 drivers tested after fatal crashes, listed at 1.10 (1.02–1.18) as a culpability study; its own adjusted odds ratio for a recorded unsafe driver action with THC alone was 1.165 (1.082–1.255), and for the driver it modelled (a 45-year-old man with no other drugs or driving record) the share with a recorded unsafe action rose from about 52 to 56 in 100 with THC (editors' calculation). These sources are not independent: the 2016 analysis re-analyses the nine studies of the 2012 review and includes the 2015 US study, so they count once. The odds ratios compare crashed with non-crashed drivers, or at-fault with not-at-fault crashed drivers, so they give no chance of a crash for any one driver; a positive test shows cannabis in the body (in blood, saliva or urine, depending on the study), not impairment; most estimates come from studies with limited adjustment; the re-analysis authors say remaining selection effects may bias the figures in either direction; and cause is not shown.
plain: Are drivers with cannabis in their body more often in crashes? Across 28 results from 21 studies, drivers with recent cannabis found in a blood, saliva or urine test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of being in a crash, or of being at fault in one, compared with drivers without it. An older review found about 1.9 times; re-checking its counts and allowing for other things brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4. When the studies allowed for alcohol, the figure was about 1.1 to 1.2. These studies compare crashed drivers with other drivers, so they cannot give the chance that any one driver crashes, and a positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.
population: Drivers in motor vehicle crashes and comparison drivers in 13 countries (United States, Australia, France, Canada, Norway, New Zealand, Netherlands, Thailand, Belgium, Denmark, Italy, Lithuania, Portugal), 1982–2015: 28 estimates from 21 case-control or culpability studies (239,739 drivers in the pooled studies), including a US analysis of 150,010 tested drivers in fatal crashes
exposure: A positive laboratory test for recent cannabis (blood, saliva or urine, or a mix, depending on the study; self-report in one)
comparator: A negative test (drivers without cannabis detected)
outcome: Being in a crash (case-control studies) or being judged responsible for a crash (culpability studies); in the US analysis, a recorded unsafe driver action
magnitude: Pooled odds ratios, 28 estimates from 21 studies (Rogeberg & Elvik, 2016; random effects; PEESE small-study regression; PEESE bias test P = 0.52; trimmed mean 1.23): 1.36 (1.15–1.61); 1.22 (1.10–1.36). Alcohol controlled (14 estimates) 1.11 (1.04–1.18) and 1.18 (1.07–1.30); not controlled (14) 1.79 (1.28–2.51) and 1.69 (1.25–2.28). High confounder adjustment (11) 1.17 (1.04–1.33) and 1.18 (1.06–1.31); limited or no adjustment (17) 1.52 (1.07–2.15) and 1.70 (1.19–2.41). Case-control (17) 1.60 and 1.32; culpability (11) 1.12 and 1.20. By quality of the measure of use: low (7) 1.07 and 1.08, medium (9) 1.81 and 1.90, high (12) 1.37 and 1.20. Study estimates 0.22 to 13.40; 17 above 1 (7 with intervals excluding 1, among them Laumon 1.43, Li 1.84, Brault 1.60 and Dubois 1.10), 9 below 1 (none excluding 1) and 2 at 1.00, editors' count from the forest plot. Earlier estimate (Asbridge et al., 2012; nine studies, crude counts, drivers with THC and no alcohol or other drug): 1.92 (1.35–2.73), I-squared 81%. Re-extraction changed four of the nine odds ratios by more than 10%, all downwards (for example 7.2 to 2.6 and 4.4 to 1.7); the revised pooled value for the same nine studies was about 1.6 with corrected counts and about 1.25–1.3 with adjusted estimates and the culpability correction (read by eye from a figure; approximate), and the authors say it lies between 1.22 and 1.36. No absolute risk is available: the studies compare crashed with non-crashed drivers or at-fault with not-at-fault drivers. If the odds ratios stood for a causal effect, (odds ratio − 1) divided by the odds ratio would give about 18 and 26 in 100 crashes involving a positive test (editors' calculation for 1.22 and 1.36; the authors say roughly 20 to 30 in 100). In the US analysis of drivers in fatal crashes (Dubois et al., 2015), THC alone at blood alcohol 0.00: odds ratio 1.165 (1.082–1.255) for a recorded unsafe driver action; 1.28 (1.21–1.36) with only blood alcohol terms in the model; for a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or driving record the share with a recorded unsafe action rose from about 52 to 56 in 100 (editors' calculation from the printed predicted odds 1.07 and 1.25).

statement: In people who came to emergency departments in Europe after taking GHB or GBL and no other drug, those reported to have also taken alcohol, compared with those not reported to have, were recorded more often with reduced consciousness and, among those admitted to hospital, more often admitted to critical care; no difference was detected in slow breathing, intubation or overall discharge. The comparison is unadjusted and alcohol use rests on report. In 609 patients at 18 centres (2013–2016; 83% from London and Oslo; 183 without and 426 with alcohol), a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 was recorded in 49 in 100 of those with data and without alcohol and 59 in 100 with it (P = 0.034; unadjusted odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.03–2.16), while a slow heart rate was recorded less often with alcohol (24 in 100 without, 16 in 100 with). Among the 219 admitted to hospital, critical care was used for 22 in 100 without alcohol (15 of 67) and 55 in 100 with it (84 of 152) (P < 0.001), about 8 and 20 in 100 of all patients in each group (editors' calculation); median time in hospital was 2 h 18 min without alcohol and 3 h 11 min with it (P < 0.001). Slow breathing (below 12 breaths a minute) was recorded in 12 in 100 without alcohol and 8 in 100 with it (odds ratio 0.68, 0.35–1.32; 21% of breathing rates missing), intubation in 4 and 6 in 100 (P = 0.32; odds ratio about 1.5, interval about 0.7–3.7, editors' rough calculation), and the two deaths (2 in 609) were both in the alcohol group, so the study could neither show nor rule out a difference in breathing or in death. In a randomized crossover study of 16 healthy adults who drank lightly and had little GHB experience, monitored in a hospital research unit, blood oxygen saturation fell most with both together, by a mean of 2.12 percentage points from baseline at 90 minutes, more than with placebo, with GHB alone (P = 0.027) or with ethanol alone (P = 0.013). The patient data come from emergency departments only, with no amounts, timing or product (GHB, GBL and 1,4-butanediol pooled), alcohol by report, toxicology in 6% of patients, no adjustment for age, sex or centre, about 33 uncorrected comparisons and missing values for several measures; the volunteer study is small, used one fixed combination, and measured oxygen saturation, a different outcome. Whether alcohol causes the differences, at what amounts, and the risk to breathing and life were not shown.
plain: Does alcohol with GHB make breathing or consciousness worse? In a European study of 609 emergency room patients who had taken GHB or GBL and no other drug, 59 in 100 of those who had also had alcohol were less awake (a Glasgow Coma Score under 13), against 49 in 100 of those who had not. Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. No difference was found in slow breathing or in needing a breathing tube, but the study could not rule one out; two people died, both had alcohol. In a small study of 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell a little more with both drugs than with either alone. In the emergency room study, alcohol use was by report and the amounts taken were not known.

statement: In 2,019 tabulated admissions (of 2,222) to one Australian regional toxicology unit after an overdose that included a serotonergic drug (1987 to 2002), the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, a rule built from seven bedside findings, compared with Sternbach's older criteria applied to the same records, agreed with the unit's own toxicologists' diagnosis of serotonin toxicity as follows: the new rule flagged 145 of the 172 people they diagnosed (84%; editors' 95% interval 78 to 89) and left 1,785 of the 1,847 they did not diagnose unflagged (97%; 95.7 to 97.4), against 129 of 172 (75%; 68 to 81) and 1,772 of 1,847 (96%; 94.9 to 96.7) for Sternbach's criteria; the paper gives no intervals and no test of the difference. In the presence of a serotonergic drug the rule says yes for clonus (rhythmic muscle jerks) that starts by itself; clonus that can be set off, or clonus of the eyes, together with agitation or sweating; tremor with brisk reflexes; or stiff muscles with a temperature above 38 °C and clonus of the eyes or that can be set off. The authors and two later narrative reviews (Boyer & Shannon, 2005; Buckley et al., 2014) describe serotonin toxicity as a spectrum from mild to life-threatening, caused by too much serotonin activity in the brain, with changes in muscles and nerves (shaking, brisk reflexes, clonus and, when severe, rigidity), in automatic body functions (sweating, fast heart rate, fever) and in mental state (agitation, confusion). Of 473 single-SSRI overdoses, 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0) were diagnosed; 6 people were put on a ventilator solely because the toxicity was worsening, all with a high fever, and increasing rigidity that impaired breathing was what led to the ventilation. The authors say a fast heart rate and wide pupils were common but also occur in other poisonings, so they are poor at telling serotonin excess apart. These were overdose admissions, so the findings do not show how the signs look at prescribed amounts or in people who are never admitted to a toxicology unit; the rule was fitted to single-SSRI overdoses that are part of the test set, so the figures may be higher than they would be in new patients; 203 admissions are missing from the main table without explanation; and the diagnosis they were scored against is the unit's own judgment, which the authors call arbitrary because there is no gold standard. Later reviews call the criteria validated while citing only this paper (Buckley et al., 2014), or call the toxicologist's diagnosis a gold standard (Boyer & Shannon, 2005); no independent test is in the sources read. Early or mild signs may be taken for ordinary drug effects (Silins et al., 2007, without data).
plain: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) means too much serotonin activity in the body, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. Doctors recognise it by examining the person. They look for muscle jerks that start on their own or can be set off (also in the eyes) together with agitation or sweating, for shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, in severe cases, for stiff muscles with a high fever. In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs picked out about 84 of every 100 people the unit's toxicologists had diagnosed, against about 75 in 100 for an older checklist, and left about 97 of every 100 people not diagnosed unflagged. But the standard was the unit's own judgment, the checklist was built on the same kind of patients it was tested on, and everyone had taken an overdose, so it may do less well in other settings. Mild signs can look like the ordinary effects of a drug. No independent test of the checklist was found in the papers read.
population: People admitted to one Australian regional toxicology unit (Hunter Area Toxicology Service, Newcastle, New South Wales) from 13 January 1987 to 22 November 2002 after an overdose that included at least one serotonergic drug: 2,222 of 9,960 admissions, of which 2,019 are in the main accuracy table; the rule was built from the 473 admissions with an overdose of one SSRI alone, which are part of the 2,222. Age was tested (p = 0.004) but its values are not given; sex, the drugs taken and the amounts are not reported. Descriptions of what serotonin toxicity is come from the paper and from two narrative reviews.
exposure: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria applied to the admission record: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, yes if spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or sweating; ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; tremor with brisk reflexes; or stiff muscles with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no
comparator: Sternbach's 1991 criteria (three or more of ten listed features, with a recent addition or increase of a serotonergic agent) applied to the same records; both sets of criteria scored against the diagnosis made by the admitting clinical toxicologist, with treatment by a 5-HT2A antagonist and Sternbach's criteria as two further reference outcomes
outcome: Agreement with the admitting toxicologist's diagnosis of serotonin toxicity (sensitivity and specificity); how often that diagnosis was made in single-SSRI overdoses; and the findings of the six people ventilated solely for worsening toxicity
magnitude: Test set against the toxicologist's diagnosis (Table 1a; 2,019 of 2,222 admissions, the other 203 not in the table): flagged and diagnosed 145; flagged but not diagnosed 62; not flagged but diagnosed 27; not flagged and not diagnosed 1,785 (172 diagnosed, 1,847 not diagnosed). Printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; the paper gives none): sensitivity 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1,785/1,812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0). Sternbach's criteria on the same records (Table 2): 1,772, 75, 43 and 129; printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%; editors' calculation from the cells: 129/172 = 75.0% (68.0 to 80.9) and 1,772/1,847 = 95.9% (94.9 to 96.7); positive predictive value 129/204 = 63.2% from the cells (69.4% if the printed column total of 186 is used). Against Sternbach's criteria as the reference (Table 1b) the Hunter rule had printed sensitivity 69% and specificity 97%; against treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist (Table 1c) 78% and 94%. No test is given for the difference between the two sets of criteria; the editors' intervals for sensitivity overlap, and the people are the same in both. Derivation set (473 single-SSRI overdoses): diagnosed by a toxicologist 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0); met Sternbach's criteria 70 (14.8%, 11.7 to 18.4); treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist 44 (9.3%, 6.8 to 12.3). Intubated: 42 for reduced consciousness or decontamination and 6 solely for worsening serotonin toxicity (6 of 2,222 = 0.27%, editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results › Decision rules, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
evidence.extracted: Figure 2, decision rules: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, serotonin toxicity is yes if (1) spontaneous clonus; (2) inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (3) ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (4) tremor with hyperreflexia; or (5) hypertonic with a temperature above 38 C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no. Seven variables were needed: spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and hyperreflexia. Rule 5 was added although the classification-tree analysis did not select it, because clonus and hyperreflexia are often not demonstrable in severe rigidity; the life-threatening cases were not in the learning dataset of SSRI-alone overdoses, because they occur with combinations of serotonergic agents.

evidence.extracted: The Hunter Area Toxicology Service is a regional toxicology unit; every overdose presentation and admission is entered prospectively into a clinical database by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses. Of 9960 admissions between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this test dataset had no exclusions and includes the derivation dataset. Derivation dataset: 473 admissions with a single SSRI, after excluding 9 with two SSRIs and any with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone, lithium or an anti-serotonergic drug taken as well. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95%CI 12.3–19.0) had a diagnosis of serotonin toxicity made by a clinical toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 95%CI 11.7–18.4) met Sternbach's criteria and 44 (9.3%, 95%CI 6.8–12.3) were treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist. The tree analysis was done in the SSRI-alone dataset; the rules were tested on the complete dataset. The paper reports no age values, sex, breakdown by drug or amounts (age was tested, p = 0.004, with no direction given).

evidence.locator: Results › Life-threatening serotonin toxicity (single paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Life-threatening cases were those intubated and ventilated. Forty-two patients were intubated for a decreased Glasgow Coma Score or for decontamination; six were intubated solely for worsening serotonin toxicity. All six had a high fever and multiple features of serotonin toxicity. Progressive rigidity compromising respiratory function was the precipitating event; the preceding signs were a high fever (above 38.5 C) and increasing, particularly truncal, rigidity and peripheral hypertonicity. Editors' calculation: 6 of 2222 admissions = 0.27%.

They state that the decision rules will need to be validated in other settings, including other toxicology treatment centres, emergency departments and psychiatric units, and studied prospectively in people taking toxic and therapeutic amounts of serotonergic drugs.

evidence.extracted: The authors write that serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum of toxicity rather than a defined clinical entity with clear prognostic importance, and so call it serotonin toxicity; that it results from an increase in serotonin in the synapses of the central nervous system, so is a concentration-dependent toxicity that can develop in any individual and not an idiosyncratic reaction; and that it can be thought of as a triad of autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status.

evidence.locator: Opening paragraph; Definition and epidemiology, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review calls the serotonin syndrome a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction, a predictable consequence of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors, with clinical manifestations from barely perceptible to lethal. It is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms may be easily overlooked.

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (p. 1114); Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 1115)
evidence.extracted: The review describes its source as the clinical findings in 2222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist's diagnosis, and says its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive (84 percent against 75 percent) and more specific (97 percent against 96 percent) than the original criteria. It does not say that the figures come from one unit or that the rules were derived in part of the same records, gives no intervals, and does not mention the source paper's statement that no gold standard exists.

evidence.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, 1st paragraph; How does it present?, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review describes serotonin syndrome, also called serotonin toxicity, as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects due to increased serotonin in the central nervous system, covering a spectrum from mild to severe. It says toxicity starts within hours of ingesting the drugs and that the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion).

evidence.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features) and 3rd paragraph (beginning The term ocular clonus)
evidence.extracted: The review calls generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) the classic feature and the key component of the Hunter criteria, which it says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited for this statement is the derivation paper (reference 13). It describes spontaneous clonus as rhythmic, large muscle contractions, often triggered by minor movements or vibrations; it says clonus in general is easily elicited with ankle dorsiflexion; and it describes ocular clonus as fine or coarse oscillations of gaze in all directions.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraphs beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state and Typically, the serotonin-toxic person
evidence.extracted: The review says people with serotonin syndrome from illicit drugs such as ecstasy usually reach emergency departments with more advanced symptoms, because some of the early, mild signs are generally seen by many people who use ecstasy as part of normal drug reactions; it cites one earlier review for this and gives no data. It describes the typical picture as agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes, with muscle spasms starting in the lower limbs and becoming generalised, then fever, sweating, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate and rapid breathing, and fixed rigidity in severe cases.

The what-it-is description rests on the paper's introduction and two narrative reviews and is marked as described. Recognition is stated as a finding about how one set of rules performed, not as instructions.
