statement: In four people who died in Finland in 2000 and 2001 (aged 18 to 23; one woman and three men), MDMA and moclobemide, a reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant that had not been prescribed to any of them, were both found in post-mortem blood, and forensic pathologists certified each death as combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs (Vuori et al., 2003, a case series with no comparison group). The authors read the sparse histories (sudden confusion, convulsions or collapse; a body temperature of 43.2 °C in the one person whose temperature is given) as consistent with serotonin syndrome, but no sign that defines it (clonus, reflexes, muscle tone, tremor) was recorded in any of the four. Blood MDMA was 1.6 to 2.1 mg/L, 4.6 to 6.0 times the top of the reference range the paper quotes (editors' calculation), and moclobemide 2.1 to 7.9 mg/L, near the top of its quoted reference range in two people (the authors call this the maximum therapeutic concentration) and 2.6 to 3.2 times the top of it in two (a moderate overdose, they say; editors' calculation). Other substances were found in the blood or urine of all four (alcohol, amphetamines, cannabis and, in one man, dextromethorphan at many times the quoted range, which the pathologist counted as a contributor), and the paper does not say whether MDMA alone at these levels could have caused the deaths. Amounts taken are unknown for three; for the fourth, aged 19, the paper states ten tablets without giving a source, and his MDMA level was similar to the others'; the paper says it is not known why the four combined the drugs. As described in narrative reviews, MDMA with an MAOI is placed at the highest level of risk among the combinations with MDMA that they rank (Silins et al., 2007, who cite these four deaths and two older case reports of MDMA with phenelzine, not read here); MAOIs are said to be strongly associated with severe cases when combined with MDMA (Boyer & Shannon, 2005); and one reviewer says that several unpublished cases are known to him (Gillman, 2005). No source read counts the people who took MDMA with an MAOI and had no such outcome, and cases are selected by death, so no rate or relative risk can be given; Silins et al. also state that only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-related serotonin syndrome have been published since the late 1980s. In a technical report summarized by Silins et al., about 1 in 25 people in an Australian study of people who use ecstasy said they had deliberately combined it with moclobemide; the review gives no sample size. People can feel little from an amount of MDMA for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more; no source read measured what happens then with an MAOI.
plain: Four young people in Finland died in 2000 and 2001 with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood. Moclobemide is an antidepressant that stops the body breaking down serotonin, and none of the four had been prescribed it. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the authors thought the signs fitted serotonin syndrome, but no examination signs were recorded. All four had MDMA levels about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes, and all had other drugs in their blood or urine, so MDMA alone cannot be ruled out. Reviews place MDMA with this kind of antidepressant at the highest risk of the mixes they rank, but nobody has counted how many people took both and had no such outcome, so no rate can be given. Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ, and some then take more; no study measured what happens then with this antidepressant. The evidence is four deaths and reviews.
population: Four people who died in Finland in 2000 and 2001 (a woman aged 18 and men aged 23, 18 and 19), identified by the authors' forensic medicine departments as appearing to be a fatal interaction of MDMA and moclobemide; moclobemide had not been prescribed to any of them. Further cases and the ranking of the combination are described second-hand in narrative reviews.
exposure: MDMA together with the reversible MAO-A inhibitor moclobemide, found in post-mortem blood (MDMA 1.6, 2.0, 1.7 and 2.1 mg/L; moclobemide 2.3, 2.1, 7.9 and 6.5 mg/L); amounts and timing taken are not known (study condition only: one man was reported to have taken ten ecstasy tablets, source not stated); other MAOIs such as phenelzine appear only as described in reviews
comparator: No comparison group: the paper describes no deaths with MDMA alone, moclobemide alone or other combinations, and nobody who took the combination and survived is counted
outcome: Death, certified by forensic pathologists as combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide; the authors' reading of the sparse histories (sudden confusion, convulsions, collapse; one temperature of 43.2 °C) as consistent with serotonin syndrome
magnitude: No rate or relative risk can be derived: four deaths selected by outcome, no denominator. Post-mortem blood (mg/L), MDMA then moclobemide: case 1 (woman, 18) 1.6 and 2.3; case 2 (man, 23) 2.0 and 2.1; case 3 (man, 18) 1.7 and 7.9; case 4 (man, 19) 2.1 and 6.5. Reference ranges quoted in the paper: MDMA 0.1 to 0.35, moclobemide 1.5 to 2.5. Editors' calculation: MDMA 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of its range; moclobemide 0.9, 0.8, 3.2 and 2.6 times the upper end of its range. Body temperature 43.2 °C in case 3 (when it was taken is not stated); none recorded for the others. As summarized by Silins et al. (2007): approximately 1 in 25 people in a recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide (a technical report by two of the review's authors; no sample size, recruitment method or time frame given).

evidence.locator: Abstract
evidence.extracted: The abstract describes four deaths following ingestion of moclobemide and MDMA, says the probable cause of death in each was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs, and infers a purpose for taking moclobemide because none of the four had been prescribed it. The pathologists' stated cause in each case, in the case descriptions, is combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the Discussion says it is not known why the victims combined the substances.

evidence.locator: Method (reference ranges; the single paragraph begins on p. 365); Case 1, Case 2, Case 3 (p. 366); Case 4 (begins at the foot of p. 366)
evidence.extracted: Reference ranges quoted in the Method: MDMA in blood 0.1–0.35 mg/l; moclobemide 1.5–2.5 mg/l. Case 1: woman aged 18, unknown quantity of street ecstasy, next morning suddenly confused, convulsed, lost consciousness and stopped breathing; no temperature taken; blood MDMA 1.6 mg/l, moclobemide 2.3 mg/l; alcohol in blood and urine; amphetamines in urine. Case 2: man aged 23 found dead after a confused state, with two kinds of white tablets that both contained MDMA; blood MDMA 2.0 mg/l, moclobemide 2.1 mg/l, dextromethorphan 1.1 mg/l (quoted range 0.01–0.04), plus morphine, amphetamine, cyclizine and several benzodiazepines; the pathologist counted dextromethorphan as contributing. Case 3: man aged 18 who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years, suddenly confused, rolled about on the floor, collapsed; body temperature of the deceased 43.2 C; blood MDMA 1.7 mg/l, amphetamine 0.15 mg/l, moclobemide 7.9 mg/l, cannabis in blood and alcohol in urine. Case 4: man aged 19 who had taken 10 ecstasy tablets, unconscious with breathing difficulties, died in hospital; no temperature; blood MDMA 2.1 mg/l, moclobemide 6.5 mg/l, cannabis, MDA and lidocaine. In all four the pathologist concluded combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide. No clonus, reflexes, tone or tremor is recorded for any. Editors' calculation: the four MDMA concentrations are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the quoted MDMA range (0.35 mg/l); moclobemide 0.9, 0.8, 3.2 and 2.6 times the upper end of its range (2.5 mg/l).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; paragraph beginning Moclobemide had not been prescribed; paragraph beginning It is not known why the victims combined these substances; last paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors say that, to their knowledge, no fatal cases of this combination had been reported before; that history and clinical observations were limited in most cases, but the mode of death in each was consistent with a serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it; that moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the victims and was present at maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and in moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4; that it is not known why the victims combined the substances; that the only known link between the cases is the region, with cases 1 and 2 close in time; that in case 2 moclobemide could also have slowed the breakdown of dextromethorphan; and that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAO inhibitor, is taken together with MDMA, a statement given without a rate or a comparison.

evidence.locator: Results › High risk, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 651, right-hand column; the 2nd paragraph ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 652)
evidence.extracted: The review places ecstasy taken with MAOI antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine), other MAOIs and the reversible inhibitor moclobemide in the high-risk group, as likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin. It says cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy with phenelzine have been reported as early as 1987 (two older case reports, not read here) and that ecstasy with moclobemide can give rise to fatalities, a handful of cases being documented (the Finnish series read here); it says further evidence that moclobemide increases the likelihood of severe serotonin syndrome with ecstasy comes from animal studies.

evidence.locator: Results › High risk, paragraph beginning In a recent Australian study (left-hand column)
evidence.extracted: Approximately one in 25 people in a recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide (a technical report by two of the review's authors; the review gives no sample size, recruitment method or time frame); the same research is said to have found that deliberately taking antidepressants with ecstasy went with a greater likelihood of reporting muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and profuse sweating.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins in the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say that since the late 1980s only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described; that the incidence of ecstasy-related fatalities seems low compared with the likely frequency of use, but the extent of acute non-fatal harm is harder to estimate because less serious cases are not usually published; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is taken together with other serotonergic drugs or substances.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 435 and ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 436)
evidence.extracted: The review states that illicit stimulants such as MDMA, if combined with MAOIs (including moclobemide), also cause fatalities because they act as serotonin releasers; that serotonin releasers with MAOIs are the only other combination, besides MAOIs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors, able to cause serotonin toxicity of a severe and potentially fatal degree; that several unpublished cases of MAOI and releaser combinations are known to the author; and that a recent case series of four deaths has been reported by Vuori (the paper read here).

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations
evidence.extracted: The review says that MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA, and cites other papers for this sentence; the Finnish series is not among the review's references.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall very high on the study card: no comparison group, other substances in every person, MDMA alone at 4.6 to 6.0 times the quoted reference range cannot be excluded, the cause of death is a judgment by authors who selected the cases, and no examination sign that defines serotonin syndrome was recorded.

indirectness.note: The primary report concerns one MAOI, moclobemide, a reversible inhibitor of MAO-A; the extension to other MAOIs and to older and unpublished cases is second-hand through narrative reviews that were not appraised.

imprecision.note: No rate or interval is claimed; the lack of a denominator is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; unreported cases are unknown.

Risk of bias -2 (ROBINS-E very high on the card), indirectness -1 (one MAOI read in a primary report, the rest second-hand through reviews); inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low (the floor). Status single study: one case series read in full; reviews that cite it do not count as further studies. Stays draft: the claim rests on one case series and on reviews (METHODS 6 and 12; brief). The relation is worded as an association in four selected deaths: that the combination caused them is not shown, because MDMA alone at these levels cannot be excluded and the clinical signs that define the syndrome were not recorded. The claim gives no rate, because none can be derived, and no instruction.

statement: As described in a 2007 narrative review of the literature to 2006 (Silins et al.), whose authors did not comment on the quality of any study and give no counts of the studies behind each group, serotonergic substances were placed in groups by how likely each is to cause serotonin syndrome when taken with ecstasy (MDMA). Substances that block the serotonin transporter (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, the painkiller tramadol, the cough-medicine ingredient dextromethorphan and some antihistamines) are called not likely to raise serotonin to life-threatening levels, because they are said to compete with MDMA and so weaken its effects; the support is that argument, animal experiments and controlled studies in which citalopram reduced ecstasy's effects (effects, not toxicity), and the trials of SSRIs with MDMA are covered in a separate claim. Other serotonin releasers (amphetamine and its derivatives, cocaine) and serotonin precursors (5-HTP, L-tryptophan) are placed at intermediate risk: the review says that high doses or repeated use of stimulants increase the risk, that serious symptoms were reported more often with amphetamine and cocaine, and, for 5-HTP, that no human case of serotonin syndrome has been reported. MAOIs are placed at high risk (a separate claim), and St John's wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs and lithium are left as unknown. The review also says that deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are relatively rare and that only a handful of case reports have been published since the late 1980s, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater with other serotonergic substances; non-fatal harm is harder to estimate. The grouping is the authors' judgment: no source read counts people who took each pair; the review's table does not show which placements rest on reports of people and which on mechanism; it places tramadol and venlafaxine with the transporter blockers although Gillman (2005), whom it cites for the group, calls both anomalous and says they may also release serotonin; and it describes methylphenidate as a potent releaser where Gillman calls it weak. Real use differs from the sources: the review says people who use ecstasy often take other serotonergic drugs on the same occasion (alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine) and that serotonergic medicines and supplements are sometimes deliberately combined with it, on anecdotal evidence. People can feel little from an amount of MDMA for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more or add another substance; the review says high doses or repeated use intensify serotonin release, but no source read measured how taking more changes the risk with each combination.
plain: A 2007 review sorted drugs by how risky they are with ecstasy (MDMA). It put antidepressants of the SSRI type, and a few painkillers and cough medicines that work the same way on serotonin, in the lower-risk group, because they blunt ecstasy's effects. It put other stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan, in the middle, and MAOI antidepressants highest. The review says deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, but that serious harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin. But the sorting is the authors' judgment from reports, animal studies and how the drugs work, not from counts: nobody has counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk with each mix.
population: People who take ecstasy (MDMA) together with other serotonergic substances, as described in a 2007 narrative review of reviews, case reports, animal studies, surveys and two controlled volunteer studies (Silins et al.); no study read counted people who took each combination
exposure: Ecstasy (MDMA) taken together with another serotonergic substance, in the review's groups: reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, tramadol, dextromethorphan, antihistamines); releasers and precursors (amphetamine and derivatives, cocaine, 5-HTP, L-tryptophan); MAOIs (a separate claim); unknown (St John's wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs, lithium). Amounts and timing are not given in the review
comparator: Ecstasy alone; no source read compared the groups with each other, or with ecstasy alone, in people
outcome: Serotonin syndrome, in the review's words life-threatening rises in serotonin or serious serotonin syndrome; no counts are given
magnitude: No counts, rates or intervals for any combination in the sources read. The review's grouping (Table 1), for use with ecstasy: less risk (SSRIs; SNRIs such as venlafaxine; tricyclic antidepressants; the opioids tramadol and dextromethorphan; antihistamines); intermediate risk (amphetamine and derivatives; cocaine; 5-HTP; L-tryptophan); high risk (MAOIs and the reversible inhibitor moclobemide; a separate claim); unknown risk (St John's wort; LSD; anti-migraine drugs; lithium). Groups follow the proportion of agreement between studies, with no study counts and no appraisal of study quality.

evidence.locator: Abstract
evidence.extracted: The abstract gives the aim as bringing together the risk of serotonin syndrome from taking ecstasy with other serotonergic substances into a hierarchy for doctors, from an extensive online database search. Findings: substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy; high doses or repeated use of stimulants such as methamphetamine and cocaine with ecstasy increase the risk, as does pharmaceutical amphetamine with ecstasy; serotonin precursors also influence the course; and substances that inhibit monoamine oxidase are most likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin with ecstasy.

evidence.locator: Method, single paragraph (right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: A review of peer-reviewed and grey literature up to 2006 using Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed, with search terms that included but were not limited to those listed (a minority from ecstasy-related websites). Substances were categorized as less, intermediate or high risk with ecstasy according to the proportion of agreement between studies; comment on the methodological quality of each study was not made; national experts were consulted when appropriate. No inclusion criteria and no count of records found or used are given.

evidence.locator: Results › Less risk, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 650; the 3rd ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 651); Table 1 (p. 651)
evidence.extracted: Substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake (SSRIs, the SNRI venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, the opioid analgesics tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines) are said not to be likely to raise serotonin to life-threatening levels with ecstasy, because they compete with MDMA at the serotonin receptor site and so diminish its effects (the wording is the review's; reuptake inhibitors act at the transporter). Controlled studies are said to find that the physiological and subjective effects of ecstasy are substantially reduced in participants given citalopram; animal experiments are said to show that some SSRIs block MDMA-induced serotonin release; whether SSRIs protect against MDMA's long-lasting neurotoxic effects in humans is said to be yet to be determined. Bupropion is said to be devoid of clinically significant serotonergic effects. Table 1 sets out the groups: less, intermediate, high and unknown risk.

evidence.locator: Results › Intermediate risk, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (left-hand column) and 4th and 5th paragraphs, on 5-HTP and L-tryptophan (right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: Because severity depends on the type and quantity of substance, ecstasy, a potent releaser of serotonin, taken with other releasers or precursors is said to be likely to carry a greater risk of serious serotonin syndrome; high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues are said to intensify serotonin release; serious serotonergic symptoms are said to have been reported more often when ecstasy is used with amphetamine and cocaine (a source not read here). Dexamphetamine and methylphenidate are called relatively potent serotonin releasers (Table 1 prints ethylphenidate), as is methamphetamine. For 5-HTP the review cites a review that found no reported human cases of serotonin syndrome, with deaths from overdose in animals, and says its use with ecstasy is in theory likely to precipitate the syndrome; for L-tryptophan it says the risk is likely to increase if it is combined with ecstasy, especially if used beforehand.

evidence.locator: Results › Unknown risk, four paragraphs (beginning The herbal extract Saint John's wort, Lysergic acid, Anti-migraine drugs and Relatively little is known about the mechanism of action of lithium)

It adds that people who use ecstasy tend to use other serotonergic illicit drugs on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy.

It says a recent review of the literature shows that, of the releasers, amphetamine is relatively potent and a risk, whereas methylphenidate is a weak releaser. statement: As described in narrative reviews, some opioid painkillers have been reported with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant in cases of serotonin toxicity, some of them fatal, and others have no reports. In a 2005 review by one author (Gillman), based on about 40 reports that are listed on his website and not in the paper, pethidine (meperidine), tramadol and dextromethorphan (a cough-medicine ingredient that he groups with these opioids) have definite reports with MAOIs, with fatalities named for each of the three (called possible for tramadol in one table), and possibly for fentanyl, which has one case and one possible death and is called uncertain; morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine have no reports. For methadone the review disagrees with itself: its abstract lists methadone among opioids involved in reactions with MAOIs, but its table says no reports are known, so methadone is not counted as reported here. He links this to how strongly each opioid blocks the serotonin transporter in laboratory tests (14.1 to 760 nM for pethidine, tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan; above 100,000 nM for the morphine group; lower is stronger; values from different sources and species); by the editors' reading, every value in the first group is above the 1 to 10 nM range he calls borderline. Boyer and Shannon (2005) state that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City resulted from pethidine (meperidine) with the MAOI phenelzine, citing a 1988 journal article whose title refers to the case, and list that pair first among seven combinations associated with severe serotonin syndrome; Buckley et al. (2014) list pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan among drugs associated with serotonin toxicity and say that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI, a conclusion from reviews of case reports, four of the six by Gillman. Limits: nine of the eleven different papers Gillman cites for fatalities date from 1955 to 1971, and one of them is a rabbit study (editors' count); where their titles name an MAOI it is iproniazid, phenelzine (also as Nardil) or, in the rabbit study, pargyline, and none names moclobemide (editors' reading); he judges the old reports by his own reading; a 1968 test of pethidine and morphine in 15 patients (by its title, in the presence of MAOIs) found no serotonergic symptoms but did not look for clonus or reflexes; no rate is given and nobody counts the people who took an opioid with an MAOI without a problem; and no reports for the morphine group is an absence of reports, not a test in people. Gillman judges the risk with the serotonergic opioids probably low but unpredictable, says any reaction is dose-related, and says enzyme differences vary blood levels 20- to 50-fold between people. People can feel little pain relief from an amount of a painkiller for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, bodies that differ), and some take more; no source read measured what happens then with an MAOI.
plain: Reports link some opioid painkillers to serious reactions when taken with MAOI antidepressants. A 2005 review by one doctor says pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan (found in cough medicines) have been involved, some of them fatal, and that fentanyl is unclear. Methadone is unclear too: the review's summary lists it, but its own table says no reports are known. Morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine had no reports, which means a lack of reports, not a test in people. The review rests on about 40 reports it does not show; the papers it cites for deaths are mostly from 1955 to 1971; and nobody has counted how often the reaction happens. The doctor thinks the risk is probably low but unpredictable, and that it depends on the amount. Some people feel little pain relief from an amount and take more, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ; no study measured what happens then with an MAOI.
population: People taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant who were given or took an opioid painkiller, as described in narrative reviews of case reports (about 40 on the main reviewer's website, not seen) and of laboratory measurements; his conclusion covers any type of MAOI, but the titles of the older fatality reports name iproniazid and phenelzine, not moclobemide
exposure: An opioid painkiller, or dextromethorphan, taken or given during MAOI treatment: pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, dextromethorphan, fentanyl, methadone; laboratory serotonin transporter values, Ki in nM (lower is stronger): pethidine 413, tramadol 760 and 528, dextromethorphan 23, methadone 270 and 14.1
comparator: Opioids that do not block the serotonin transporter appreciably (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine; values above 100,000 nM), for which no reports were found; there is no comparison in people
outcome: Reports of serotonin toxicity, some fatal, in published case reports as the main review counts and reads them; no rate
magnitude: No rate or relative risk is given in any source read. As described by Gillman (2005): about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity involving analgesics (list on the author's website, not seen). Serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; lower is stronger; values from different sources and species cannot be compared directly): morphine 500,000 and over 100,000; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000; pethidine 413; tramadol 760 and 528; dextromethorphan 23; methadone 270 and 14.1. Reports with MAOIs (his Table 2): morphine, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone none; pethidine definite, with some fatalities; tramadol definite, with possible fatalities; dextromethorphan definite; fentanyl uncertain (one case and one possible death); remifentanil no case or death; pentazocine no reports known; methadone no reports known, but unlikely. Editors' count from the printed reference list: nine of the eleven different papers cited for fatalities are dated 1955 to 1971 (one is a rabbit study); the other two are from 1986 and 1992.

evidence.locator: Abstract (4th and 5th sentences, and the last two sentences)
evidence.extracted: The abstract says the phenylpiperidine series opioids pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan, and propoxyphene, appear to be weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors and have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities), and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs. It also says that only combinations of serotonergic drugs acting by different mechanisms can raise serotonin to a life-threatening level, and that the combination that most commonly does so is an MAOI with any reuptake inhibitor.

evidence.locator: Table 1 and its caption; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Table 2, serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; a lower value means higher potency; the caption says the values come from different sources and species and cannot be compared directly) and reports with MAOIs: morphine 500 000 (other references) and >100 000 (Codd), none; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone >100 000, none; tramadol 760 and 528, definite, and possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413 weak, anomalous, definite, and some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain, one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death reported; remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known, but unlikely. The Table 1 caption says fatalities from serotonin toxicity involving analgesics have been with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Overall, there is a strong association
evidence.extracted: The reviewer states that binding affinities at the serotonin transporter of less than 1 nM are invariably associated with the ability to precipitate toxicity with MAOIs and that potencies in the 1–10 nM range are borderline; that tramadol and venlafaxine are anomalous because their estimated potency suggests they should not be a risk, and that there is evidence they also act as serotonin releasers; and that pethidine, a very weak reuptake inhibitor, shows a large discrepancy that could possibly be accounted for by serotonin releasing properties, although there is no direct evidence. Editors' reading: every Table 2 value for pethidine, tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan (14.1 to 760 nM) is above the 1–10 nM borderline range.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved (begins at the foot of p. 436 and continues on p. 437)
evidence.extracted: The reviewer says the early drugs involved in these interactions (pethidine and imipramine) are weak reuptake inhibitors and, because there is a dose–effect relationship, usually fail to produce a reaction. He describes a 1968 experiment (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order (study condition: top single pethidine dose 75 mg, morphine 7.5 mg); none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak reuptake inhibitors like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible individuals or with particularly large doses. He says the complete list of references on serotonin toxicity and analgesics, located through a search of the listed papers and standard databases (approximately 40), is on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities, and the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics also some fatalities; that a small series using usual therapeutic doses may lead to a false sense of security because the dose–effect relationship is not sufficiently appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20–50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraphs beginning The limited available clinical and experimental data agree, Details of all cases involving analgesics and There are a few individual case reports (right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: The reviewer says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine) are not reuptake inhibitors, none precipitates serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and there are no reports with them; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline, weak reuptake inhibitors, implicated in multiple reports that are almost certainly serotonin toxicity as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports; that about 40 cases involving analgesics are in his updated review; and that all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports but none of the drugs without reuptake-inhibiting capacity have. For fentanyl he judges one case report with a fatality (cardiac surgery in a patient on MAOIs) probably a result of serotonin toxicity and another possibly an unrecognised case, says there is a question mark over fentanyl, that it has probably been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs without a problem, and that there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk.

evidence.locator: Conclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The conclusion says morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and that pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone definitely are weak reuptake inhibitors and may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent serotonin toxicity with any type of MAOI, but perhaps only in large doses or susceptible individuals. The ability to estimate the risk is said to be compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data; for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no reuptake affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of clinical reports are used. The reviewer writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved, sentences on fatalities (p. 437); reference list, entries 14, 31, 48, 53, 57 to 60, 63, 64, 69 and 70 (pp. 440–441)
evidence.extracted: The sentences naming fatalities cite six papers for pethidine and six for the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics, one paper appearing in both lists. The printed reference list shows reference 31 to be a study of fatal hyperthermia in rabbits, reference 60 to be titled as a paper on malignant hyperthermia with hypocalcaemia, reference 53 to be titled MAO inhibitors and coronary artery surgery: a patient death, and reference 14 (the 1968 experiment) to be titled The use of pethidine and morphine in the presence of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Editors' reading of the titles of the eleven papers: where a title names an MAOI it is iproniazid, phenelzine (also under its brand name Nardil) or, in the rabbit study, pargyline; none names moclobemide. Editors' count from the printed reference list: of the eleven different papers cited for fatalities, nine date from 1955 to 1971 and two from 1986 and 1992.

evidence.locator: Opening paragraph (final sentence, p. 1112); reference 4 (pp. 1119–1120)
evidence.extracted: The review states that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City more than 20 years earlier resulted from coadministration of meperidine (pethidine) and phenelzine (an MAOI) and calls it the most widely recognized example of this preventable condition. Its only support is reference 4, a 1988 article in the same journal whose title refers to the case itself; the review does not discuss how the cause of death was established.

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations (p. 1113); Table 1 (p. 1114)
evidence.extracted: The review says MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA. Its Table 1 lists the analgesics meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol and pentazocine among drugs associated with the syndrome, and phenelzine and meperidine as the first of seven combinations listed under drug interactions associated with severe serotonin syndrome, with no counts for any pair.

evidence.locator: Box 1 and its footnote; How do we diagnose it?, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Box 1 lists drugs associated with moderate to severe serotonin toxicity: among MAOIs, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid, isocarboxazid, moclobemide, linezolid and methylene blue; and, among serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the opioid analgesics pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan. The footnote says severe toxicity generally involves a combination of agents from different drug classes. The text calls the serotonergic actions of drugs not marketed as serotonergic, such as tramadol and fentanyl, a trap for the unwary.

evidence.locator: How can we prevent it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning An awareness of drugs with potent serotonergic effects)
evidence.extracted: The review says it is apparent from systematic reviews of case reports (six references) that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and that the relatively small number of these can easily be committed to memory. Editors' count from the reference list: four of the six cited reviews are by Gillman, one of them the 2005 review on opioids and MAOIs.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative reviews that did not appraise the underlying reports: the old reports are read against the modern definition by the reviewer's subjective interpretation; the count and nature of the fatalities cannot be checked from the paper (the case list is on a website, and a rabbit study and a paper titled on malignant hyperthermia are among the references for deaths); the 1968 experiment did not look for the signs in question.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the opioid statements rest on one review, and the reviews that repeat them cite it. The methadone inconsistency within the review is stated in the claim.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the case reports, the 1968 experiment and the transporter measurements were not read; transporter values are indirect evidence for what happens in people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review itself says that uneventful uses of fentanyl with MAOIs are probably unreported, so reports of problems may be over-represented.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the evidence is descriptive or consists of reports, and the rating is already at the floor (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Case reports and laboratory values seen only through narrative reviews start from the design of the primary studies (observational reports: low) and are downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable) and indirectness (second-hand) (METHODS 6.3): very low (the floor). The relation is worded as an association in reports: reports without a denominator cannot show that the opioids cause the reactions, and the reviewer himself says the basis for an accurate estimate of the risk is insufficient. Status single study: Gillman's review is the source of the opioid statements, Buckley et al. cite it among six reviews, and Boyer and Shannon's single-death statement rests on one 1988 article they cite without describing it, so the reviews do not count as independent. Stays draft: the claim rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The methadone statement follows the review's table and not its abstract. No advice in the sources is used.

statement: In one double-blind laboratory study of 8 adults who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, adding alcohol to repeated cocaine doses was associated with a higher heart rate, roughly 13% to 15% more cocaine in the blood over the session, and cocaethylene, a substance the body makes only when both drugs are present. In 8-hour inpatient sessions, with four nasal cocaine doses 30 minutes apart (1 mg per kg each) and oral alcohol dosed to hold the blood level near 100 mg/dL (study conditions, not amounts to use), heart rate was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .002; about 84 against 74 beats a minute averaged over the session, an editors' calculation from the printed areas under the curve). Cocaine exposure was higher with alcohol (p = .035), and cocaethylene, never found with either drug alone, cleared more slowly than cocaine (half-life 156 against 85 minutes). People rated feeling good more highly with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .04) but did not rate any high significantly higher (p = .09), and blood pressure did not differ detectably from cocaine alone; blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at the one time point reported). A narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies, which includes this one, describes second-hand up to 30% more blood cocaine, cocaethylene only with both drugs, and heart-rate rises that were additive with a trend towards greater than additive; it also describes one 6-person study in which alcohol came 30 minutes after cocaine and blood cocaine did not rise. The review adds that no retrospective study it covers shows unequivocally that the combination harms the heart more, and that one emergency-room study of over 1,000 patients found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one. The study had 8 people, gave cocaine by the nose to people who usually smoked it, and counted p below .05 one-tailed as significant across 15 measures without correction, so the heart-rate result is the sturdiest and the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results would not reach .05 on a two-tailed test (an editors' calculation). It reports no heart events or rhythm findings, cannot say whether the heart-rate rise came from the extra cocaine or from cocaethylene, and cannot show what happens outside a ward. In a second double-blind laboratory study, adults who used cocaine and alcohol were given cocaine into a vein together with alcohol (cocaine 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg per kg; study conditions, not amounts to use): cocaethylene appeared at every cocaine dose but stayed far below cocaine in the same sessions (peaks 16.8, 30.1 and 53.1 against 250, 438 and 891 ng/mL), peaked later and cleared more slowly (half-life about 2.5 against about 1.8 hours), and none formed from cocaine was detectable when cocaine was given without alcohol. In the 6 people who took cocaine 1.2 mg per kg both with and without alcohol, alcohol did not raise cocaine exposure over the session (1030 against 1010 h x ng/mL) or its peak (968 against 823 ng/mL), although cocaine's half-life was longer with alcohol (1.91 against 1.29 hours); the blood peak of benzoylecgonine, the breakdown product urine tests look for, was lower with alcohol (452 against 652 ng/mL) and its urine concentration was about half (7,770 against 14,800 ng/mL), while whether less of it was formed is not shown by these figures. Those same 6 people rated drug liking and total intoxication higher across time, but not at their peak, with alcohol than with cocaine alone; that cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized and came 1 to 3 months later, and a tracer dose of labelled cocaethylene was given in every session, so no session was free of cocaethylene (Harris et al., 2003). Cocaethylene is found in people's blood after combined use: in 7 post-mortem samples, sent to a laboratory because peaks suggesting cocaethylene had already been seen in them, it ran from 73 to 1447 ng/mL and exceeded cocaine in 4; that selection also means the range is not a sample of deaths involving both drugs. Among emergency-department samples, 10 of 17 that contained a cocaine breakdown product and alcohol held cocaethylene, while of 14 that contained cocaine but no alcohol 13 held none and one a trace, and incubation tests showed that it did not form in samples after collection under the conditions tested. Those 7 deaths have no stated cause, no comparison deaths and no denominator, so they show presence, never cause (Jatlow et al., 1991). What cocaethylene itself contributes to the combination is untested in the sources read: none of them gave it on its own, none measured a heart event or a rhythm problem, and none separated its effects from the cocaine and alcohol that produce it.
plain: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are taken together? The body makes cocaethylene, a substance that forms only when both drugs are present. In a study of 8 adults who took cocaine by the nose with alcohol on a hospital ward, heart rate was higher with both drugs than with cocaine alone, about 84 beats a minute against 74, and there was roughly 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood. In a second study, where cocaine went into a vein with alcohol, cocaethylene formed again but stayed far below the cocaine level, cleared more slowly, and was not found when cocaine was given without alcohol; in the 6 people who took cocaine both ways, alcohol did not raise how much cocaine was in the blood. Those people said they liked the drug more, and felt more intoxicated, with both drugs than with cocaine alone, but their highest ratings did not clearly differ. Cocaethylene has been found in the blood of people who used both drugs, sometimes at higher levels than cocaine, including after deaths, but those tests cannot show what caused a death. These were small hospital studies, none measured heart attacks or rhythm problems, and none of them shows what cocaethylene on its own does.
population: Two small groups of adults tested in laboratories, and selected blood samples from people who had used both drugs. Eight non-treatment-seeking adults (4 men, 4 women; mean age 33) who were already using cocaine and alcohol together and met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse, tested as hospital inpatients; the review adds 14 prospective laboratory studies of 6 to 34 people each (13 with 12 or fewer), this one among them, described second-hand; adults who used cocaine and alcohol given intravenous cocaine with alcohol, 6 of whom also took cocaine 1.2 mg per kg without alcohol in a later, unblinded session (Harris et al., 2003); 7 post-mortem blood samples selected because cocaethylene peaks had already been seen in them, and 31 emergency-department samples selected by their cocaine and alcohol results (Jatlow et al., 1991)
exposure: Four intranasal cocaine doses (1 mg per kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g per kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg per kg at 60 minutes, aimed at a blood level near 100 mg/dL), given on a ward; intravenous cocaine at 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg per kg with alcohol, with a labelled cocaethylene tracer in every session (Harris et al., 2003); study conditions only
comparator: The same people on other days with the same cocaine and a placebo drink, and with placebo cocaine (lactose) and the same alcohol; there was no session with both drugs replaced by placebo, and they knew the three conditions would occur, in random order; in Harris et al. (2003), cocaine 1.2 mg per kg alone in an unblinded, non-randomized session 1 to 3 months later, in 6 people; in Jatlow et al. (1991), samples containing cocaine but no alcohol
outcome: Heart rate and blood pressure over 8 hours, ratings of any high, feeling good and other effects, and blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol; blood and urine levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and benzoylecgonine, with heart rate, blood pressure and ratings in the same sessions; the presence and concentration of cocaethylene in blood samples from people who had used both drugs

risk_of_bias.note: Double-blind, within-person, random order, with objectively measured heart rate and drug levels; but participants knew the three possible conditions and alcohol is hard to mask, every test was counted as significant at .05 one-tailed across 15 measures without correction, and several results are printed without values (clinician ratings, six rating items, blood alcohol); the study card rates the risk of bias high overall. The second laboratory study is also rated high on its card (RoB 2): its comparison with cocaine alone rests on an open, non-randomized session held 1 to 3 months later in 6 people, and a labelled cocaethylene tracer was present in every session. The 7 post-mortem samples of Jatlow et al. (1991) were sent to the laboratory because cocaethylene peaks had already been seen in them, with no cause of death, comparison deaths or denominator.

inconsistency.note: Two primary laboratory studies and one analytical series of human samples point the same way on cocaethylene forming only when both drugs are present, and the two laboratory studies agree on heart rate; the one disagreement, whether alcohol raises blood cocaine (up to 30% higher with intranasal cocaine, no difference with intravenous cocaine), follows the route of administration, which both sets of authors give as the explanation. The review's emergency-room data show no clear excess of heart problems, which the claim also says.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim is limited to what was measured in these sessions and says that other routes, other settings and heart events are not covered.

imprecision.note: Eight people and no intervals for the contrasts; the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results (p = .035 and .04, about .07 and .08 doubled) are fragile, and only the heart-rate result (p = .002) is large relative to its spread. The second laboratory study prints P thresholds without intervals or effect sizes and rests on 6 people for its comparison with cocaine alone, so none of its null findings can be read as showing no difference.

grade.reasoning: A double-blind, within-person laboratory study with random order of conditions starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1: unmasked alcohol, one-tailed uncorrected tests across 15 measures and results printed without values in the first study; an unblinded, non-randomized comparator session months later in the second. Imprecision -2: 8 people in the first study and 6 in the second study's comparison with cocaine alone, no intervals, and fragile results for cocaine exposure and feel good. Inconsistency 0: the one disagreement, whether alcohol raises blood cocaine, follows the route (found with intranasal cocaine, not with intravenous), which the authors of both studies give as the explanation. Indirectness 0 as worded. Certainty very low. Status replicated: that cocaethylene forms only when both drugs are present is found by two independent groups (McCance-Katz et al., 1998; Harris et al., 2003) and in selected human samples by a third report that shares an investigator with the first (Jatlow et al., 1991), and a higher heart rate with the combination than with cocaine alone is found in two of them, the second in an unblinded session. Not counted as independent: Jatlow et al. (1991) and McCance-Katz et al. (1998) share an investigator, and the narrative review includes the first study. The claim does not say that the effects are more than additive, and it does not say that the combination raises the chance of a heart attack or a rhythm problem, which none of the sources read measured; what cocaethylene itself adds is untested here, since no source read gave it on its own. statement: In a narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies, whose own primary studies have not been read here, people given cocaine with alcohol did not rate themselves as more drunk than with alcohol alone; every figure on drunkenness below is second-hand from that review. As described by the review: in three studies cocaine produced a slight decrease in rated drunkenness (the review's table calls the fall non-significant in two of them) and in one it had no effect, while ratings of the cocaine high, or of global intoxication, were greater in six studies when alcohol came before or with the cocaine (in one of the six, the multiple-dose study read in full, the rise in rated any high fell short of significance, p = .09). Cocaine also lessened some alcohol-related deficits on laboratory tests (digit-symbol substitution, sedation, learning and psychomotor tasks), and blood alcohol with cocaine was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in four. The four studies behind the drunkenness ratings had 8 to 11 people each. In the one multiple-dose study read in full, in which 8 adults took four nasal cocaine doses with oral alcohol on a ward (study conditions, not amounts to use), blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at the one time point reported), no rating of drunkenness was reported at all, and a rating of feeling sleepy did not differ. The same review reports that 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain tested positive for both drugs, which it reads as no definitive protection from the impairing effects of alcohol, and it describes no study that asked other people how drunk someone who had taken both appeared. The laboratory studies in the review had 6 to 34 people each (13 of the 14 had 12 or fewer) and measured self-ratings and task scores in a laboratory. No study read asked other people how drunk someone appeared, or tested driving, so none shows how drunk someone looks to others or how they would drive.
plain: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk? In small laboratory studies gathered by one review, people given cocaine with alcohol did not say they felt more drunk than with alcohol alone, and in three studies they said they felt slightly less drunk, though two of those three falls were too small to be clear. Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about 10 percent lower. These figures are second-hand: the studies behind them have not been read here, and each had 8 to 11 people. In the one study read in full, which gave cocaine by the nose with alcohol to 8 adults, people were never asked how drunk they felt. No study asked other people how drunk someone looked, or tested driving, and some drivers who died in crashes had both drugs in their blood, so the mix did not protect them from alcohol.
population: Adults in prospective laboratory studies of alcohol with cocaine, 6 to 34 people each (13 of 14 studies with 12 or fewer; the four studies that rated drunkenness had 8 to 11 each), as described second-hand in one narrative review; 8 non-treatment-seeking adults who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, tested as hospital inpatients in the one multiple-dose study read in full, which took no rating of drunkenness; fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County (600) and Spain (285)
exposure: Cocaine (taken by the nose or injected, never smoked) with alcohol, mostly given before or with the cocaine, in doses set by the researchers and listed in the review's Table 1; in the study read in full, four intranasal cocaine doses (1 mg per kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol; study conditions only
comparator: The same people given alcohol alone, or alcohol with a cocaine placebo (laboratory studies, as the review describes them); in the study read in full, the same cocaine with a placebo drink and placebo cocaine with the same alcohol; drivers who died with alcohol alone (retrospective records)
outcome: Self-rated drunkenness or alcohol intoxication and rated high, scores on tests of learning and movement, blood alcohol, and the presence of both drugs in fatally injured drivers
magnitude: No effect size is reported for rated drunkenness. Pennings et al. (2002), second-hand: slight decrease in rated drunkenness with cocaine in three studies (Farre 1993, 9 people; Higgins 1993, 8; Farre 1997, 8; Table 1 labels the Farre falls non-significant) and no effect in one (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, 11); rated cocaine high or global intoxication greater with alcohol before or with cocaine in six studies (the review's list includes McCance-Katz et al. 1998, in which any high was short of significance, p = .09); blood alcohol unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, non-significantly, in four; alcohol-induced deficits lessened by cocaine in digit-symbol substitution, sedation, and learning and psychomotor performance; 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain positive for both drugs (editors' calculation: about 4 in 100 in each study). The review's 14 prospective studies had 6 to 34 people each, 13 of them 12 or fewer (editors' count from Table 1). McCance-Katz et al. (1998): plasma alcohol 99 (SE 7) against 118 (10) mg/dL 90 minutes into the session, p = .008; no drunkenness rating reported; sleepy not significantly different.

statement: As described second-hand by two narrative reviews (no primary study of this was read), tolerance to opioids is thought to fall during a period without them, so that a dose that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. Neither review gives an estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. White and Irvine (1999) offer the idea as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings.
plain: Does tolerance drop after a break from opioids? Two review articles suggest it does: after a period without opioids, a dose that used to feel usual may have a much stronger effect, including on breathing, and that may be one reason the chance of an overdose is higher when use starts again. But the reviews give no numbers for how long a break has to be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk goes up, and the main study behind the idea was one on hair samples. One review names time in prison or detox as examples; the other review it relies on does not mention them. Even people who have used opioids for a long time may keep some risk of slowed breathing, according to two studies in people on methadone. These are reviews of other people's work, not new studies, so this is an outline of what is known.
population: People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read
exposure: A period without opioids (a period of abstinence in the reviews' wording) before use starts again
comparator: Continued regular use; the same person's tolerance before the break
outcome: Tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression, and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
magnitude: No estimate in either source. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.

It cites one study (Tagliaro and colleagues, 1998) that found less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which it reads as suggesting a period of lower than normal use, and so lost tolerance, before death, and says that information on the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is sparse. It adds that the loss is likely to be non-uniform between effects and may be quite rapid, since receptor changes can take place in minutes or hours.
